claims.evidence: Consider referral to a nephrologist or paediatric nephrologist when eGFR is 30 ml/min/1.73 m2 or less in adults, children and young people who have recovered from an acute kidney injury. [2013]

claims.claim: Referral to a paediatric nephrologist should be considered after AKI recovery for hypertension, impaired renal function or 1+ or greater proteinuria.
claims.evidence: Consider referral to a paediatric nephrologist for children and young people who have recovered from an episode of acute kidney injury but have hypertension, impaired renal function or 1+ or greater proteinuria on dipstick testing of an early morning urine sample. [2013]

claims.claim: Urine dipstick testing for blood, protein, leucocytes, nitrites and glucose should be performed as soon as AKI is suspected or detected.
claims.evidence: Perform urine dipstick testing for blood, protein, leucocytes, nitrites and glucose in all people as soon as acute kidney injury is suspected or detected.

claims.claim: The study retrospectively used data from 76,032 adults undergoing non-cardiac surgery at Asan Medical Center (March 2019–February 2021) plus 5512 VitalDB patients for external validation.
claims.evidence: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using data from 76,032 adults who underwent non-cardiac surgery at a single tertiary medical center between March 2019 and February 2021, and used data from 5512 patients from the VitalDB open dataset for external model validation.

claims.claim: AKI was defined per KDIGO as a 1.5-fold creatinine rise from preoperative baseline or a 0.3 mg/dL rise over 48 h, measured within 7 days after surgery.
claims.evidence: AKI is defined as either a 1.5-fold increase in the creatinine level from the preoperative baseline or a rise of 0.3 mg/dL over a 48 h period, as measured within the first 7 days after surgery, in accordance with the definition from the Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines.

claims.claim: If no postoperative creatinine was measured, AKI was assumed not to have occurred.
claims.evidence: If no creatinine level was measured postoperatively, it was assumed that an AKI had not occurred.

claims.claim: Exclusions were age under 18, cardiac surgery, end-stage renal disease, and preoperative creatinine above 4.5 mg/dL.
claims.evidence: We excluded pediatric patients under the age of 18, individuals who underwent cardiac surgery, and those who were diagnosed with end-stage renal disease or had preoperative creatinine levels exceeding 4.5 mg/dL

claims.claim: Postoperative AKI incidence was 3.1% (2314/76,032) internally and 1.5% (78/5512) in the VitalDB external dataset.
claims.evidence: a total of 2314 (3.1%) patients experienced postoperative AKI. Conversely, for the external validation dataset from VitalDB, which included 5512 patients who did not meet the exclusion criteria, 78 (1.5%) developed postoperative AKI

claims.claim: GBM using all features achieved the best internal validation performance: AUROC 0.868, AUPRC 0.786, F1 0.723.
claims.evidence: the GBM algorithm had the highest prediction performance when using all the datasets, with an AUROC of 0.868, AUPRC of 0.786, and F1-score of 0.723

claims.claim: GBM with intraoperative data alone reached internal AUROC 0.816 and AUPRC 0.715.
claims.evidence: The GBM algorithm also had the highest performance when utilizing the intraoperative dataset, with an AUROC of 0.816 and AUPRC of 0.715

claims.claim: Best external validation performance was GBM on preoperative data with AUROC 0.769 and AUPRC 0.696.
claims.evidence: The external validation results for the AKI model on the VitalDB dataset showed the highest prediction performance, with an AUROC of 0.769 and AUPRC of 0.696, was achieved by the GBM algorithm when using the preoperative dataset

claims.claim: LR had the highest external F1-score (0.627) when using the entire feature set.
claims.evidence: the LR algorithm exhibited the highest prediction performance when utilizing the entire dataset, with an F1-score of 0.627

claims.claim: SHAP analysis identified total surgery time, intraoperative blood pressure, gender, preoperative albumin and creatinine as the most influential features.
claims.evidence: An analysis of the feature importance of the AKI prediction model using SHAP values on the internal dataset showed that total surgery time and intraoperative blood pressure data were highly significant, whereas the gender status from the demographic data, and albumin and creatinine levels in the preoperative laboratory test data, played pivotal roles in the prediction performance

claims.claim: Blood pressure artifacts were removed with thresholds SBP >300 or <20 mm Hg, DBP >225 or <5 mm Hg, and SBP < DBP + 5 mm Hg.
claims.evidence: Blood pressure measurements exceeding the following thresholds were excluded from the analysis: a systolic blood pressure greater than 300 mm Hg or less than 20 mm Hg, diastolic blood pressure greater than 225 mm Hg or less than 5 mm Hg, and systolic blood pressure less than the diastolic blood pressure + 5 mm Hg

claims.claim: Missing values were imputed with the mean value of each variable because missingness showed no specific pattern.
claims.evidence: Since the missing values in the modeling dataset did not exhibit any specific pattern or correlation, we addressed them by inputting the missing values with the mean value of each variable in the dataset

claims.claim: Datasets were split into training, testing, and validation sets in a 6:2:2 ratio with bootstrapping for evaluation.
claims.evidence: We divided the datasets for modeling into training, testing, and validation datasets in a ratio of 6:2:2.

claims.claim: Four modeling methods were compared: logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting machine, and a five-layer deep neural network.
claims.evidence: we employed four predictive modeling methods: logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), gradient boosting machine (GBM), and a simple deep neural network (DNN) with five layers.

claims.claim: In the AKI group anesthesia time averaged 301.9 min versus 167.4 min in the non-AKI group.
The AKI group had lower preoperative eGFR (85.0 vs 92.7 mL/min/1.73 m2) and higher creatinine (1.0 vs 0.8 mg/dL).
The achieved AUC of 0.87 surpassed a previous study's AUC of 0.82.
claims.evidence: we enhanced the postoperative AKI prediction performance, achieving an AUC of 0.87, which surpassed the previous study’s AUC of 0.82

claims.claim: A limitation is that only statistical summaries of intraoperative blood pressure, not the full time series, were used for modeling.
claims.evidence: we did not use the complete intraoperative blood pressure (BP) dataset for the predictive modeling; instead, we utilized statistical summaries of the BP data.

claims.claim: The primary endpoint was prediction of AKI stage 3 lasting at least 72 h in the ICU, in adult patients classified as KDIGO AKI stage 2 or 3.
claims.evidence: We selected adult patients admitted to ICU classified as AKI stage 2 or 3 as defined by the "Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes" criteria. The primary endpoint was the ability to predict AKI stage 3 lasting for at least 72 h while in the ICU.

claims.claim: 7759 ICU patients were enrolled; persistent stage 3 AKI incidence was 11% in development, 6% in internal validation, and 19% in external validation cohorts.
claims.evidence: A total of 7759 ICU patients were enrolled for analysis. The incidence of persistent stage 3 AKI varied from 11 to 6% in the development and internal validation cohorts, respectively and 19% in external validation cohorts.

claims.claim: The model achieved auROC 0.94 (95% CI 0.92–0.95) in the US external validation cohort and 0.85 (95% CI 0.83–0.88) in the Italian external validation cohort.
claims.evidence: The model achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.94 (95% CI 0.92–0.95) in the US external validation cohort and 0.85 (95% CI 0.83–0.88) in the Italian external validation cohort.

claims.claim: The definition of persistent AKI stage 3 has not been unanimously accepted, unlike KDIGO AKI staging formalized in 2012.
claims.evidence: While the definition of AKI and its staging has been formalized by the "Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes" (KDIGO) organization during its 2012 annual conference [21], the definition of persistent AKI stage 3 has not been unanimously accepted.

claims.claim: pAKI3 is defined as AKI stage 3 lasting >=72 h (T72), or AKI stage 3 >=48 h leading to death (D48), or RRT initiated after >24 h of AKI stage 3 excluding stage 3 solely attributed to RRT (RRT24).
claims.evidence: we defined Persistent AKI Stage 3 (pAKI3) as a combination of AKI Stage 3, lasting at least 72 h (T72) or AKI Stage 3 lasting at least 48 h and leading to death (D48) or the initiation of renal replacement therapy after more than 24 h of AKI Stage 3, excluding cases where Stage 3 was solely attributed to RRT (RRT24).

claims.claim: Patients without renal recovery within 3–7 days had reduced 1-year survival (40% vs 90%) and increased risk of chronic renal disease.
claims.evidence: patients without renal recovery within 3–7 days showed reduced survival over the following year (40% vs 90%) and increased risk of developing chronic renal disease than those who recovered renal function [4].

claims.claim: Inclusion required adult (>=18 years) ICU patients with recorded sex, height and weight, and concomitant sCr and UO measurement starting in the first 12 h of ICU stay.
claims.evidence: We included ICU adult (≥ 18 years of age) patients having recorded sex, height, and weight. To assess KDIGO staging, concomitant measurement of serum creatinine (sCr) and urine output (UO) starting in the first 12 h of the ICU stay were required.

claims.claim: AKI stage was computed at any hour using the last sCr measurement and the last 24 h of urine output; only stays with at least one hour of AKI stage 2 were selected.
claims.evidence: By looking at the last sCr measurement and the last 24 h of urine output we computed the AKI stage at any hour of any stay; then we selected only those stays having at least one hour marked as AKI stage 2

claims.claim: Exclusion criteria included age <18 years, height <130 cm or >200 cm, renal transplant at admission, less than 24 h of data, and oliguria (no anuria) at start of data.
claims.evidence: Demographic exclusion Age < 18 years Height < 130 cm and > 200 cm Renal Transplant at admission Staging exclusion Less than 24 h of data Oliguria (no Anuria) at start of data

claims.claim: Imminence exclusions were death after less than 48 h of AKI stage 3 and RRT after less than 24 h of AKI stage 3.
claims.evidence: Imminence Exclusion Death after less than 48 h of AKI stage 3 RRT after less than 24 h of AKI stage 3

claims.claim: Baseline serum creatinine was the nadir sCr: minimum sCr between admission and RRT initiation for RRT stays, otherwise minimum sCr among all non-RRT patient stays.
claims.evidence: The baseline serum creatinine (bSCr) was established by modifying the nadir serum creatinine (sCr). For ICU stays with RRT, we chose the minimum sCr between admission and RRT initiation. For stays without RRT, the minimum sCr among all patient-related stays was selected, excluding those involving RRT.

claims.claim: The nadir baseline approach achieved 81.7% sensitivity and 79.8% specificity for AKI diagnosis versus pre-hospital baseline, with only 2.8% misclassified as KDIGO stage 2 or 3.
claims.evidence: This approach was found to achieve 81.7% sensitivity and a specificity of 79.8% for the diagnosis of AKI, when compared with actual pre-hospital admission baseline values, and only 2.8% misclassified KDIGO stage 2 or 3 [30, 31].

claims.claim: Thirteen variables were selected: serum creatinine, urine output, hematocrit, hemoglobin, bicarbonate, blood urea nitrogen, chloride, glucose, heart rate, platelets, potassium, sodium, white blood cell count.
claims.evidence: The selection procedure described in section "Model performances" identified: serum creatinine, urine output, hematocrit, hemoglobin, bicarbonate, blood urea nitrogen, chloride, glucose, heart rate, platelets, potassium, sodium, white blood cells count.

claims.claim: Cohort sizes and pAKI3 incidences were 1607 stays/11.2% (AmsterdamUMCdb), 1497/11.4% (MIMIC-III), 3562/5.7% (eICU), 1093/18.6% (MargheritaTre), from 345,927 ICU admissions.
claims.evidence: starting from a total of 345,927 ICU admissions we obtained: 1607 stays and 11.2% incidence in the AmsterdamUMCdb, 1497 stays and 11.4% incidence in the MIMIC-III, 3562 stays and 5.7% incidence in the eICU dataset coming from 139 centers, and 1093 stays and 18.6% incidence in the MargheritaTre dataset from 16 centers.

claims.claim: At a threshold set for 80% sensitivity on internal validation, eICU performance was 0.93 sensitivity, 0.82 specificity, 0.24 precision; MargheritaTre 0.73 sensitivity, 0.78 specificity, 0.43 precision.
claims.evidence: For the eICU dataset the same working point corresponds to 0.93 sensitivity, 0.82 specificity and 0.24 precision. For MargheritaTre we achieve 0.73 sensitivity, 0.78 specificity and 0.43 precision.

claims.claim: Internal validation auROC was 0.90 (AmsterdamUMCdb) and 0.93 (MIMIC-III), with auPR 0.48 and 0.54.
claims.evidence: In the internal AmsterdamUMCdb and MIMIC-III validation cohort the model achieved auROC 0.90 and 0.93 respectively, while it reached auPR 0.48 and 0.54.

claims.claim: A creatinine-only baseline model achieved auROC 0.91 in eICU and 0.83 in MargheritaTre, with auPR 0.29 and 0.45.
claims.evidence: a model using the lone creatinine as biomarker achieved 0.91 auROC in eICU and 0.83 in MargheritaTre, while its auPR was 0.29 and 0.45 respectively

claims.claim: The model used a 542-component feature vector per timestamp, of which only 214 features had non-null importance after L1 regularization.
claims.evidence: Thanks to the high L1 regularization parameter, out of the 542 features only 214 have a non-null feature importance.

claims.claim: Fairness analysis found AOD outside the optimal [-0.1, 0.1] range for trauma (-0.23), sepsis (-0.27), cancer (-0.38), young age 18-39 (0.21), Asian ethnicity (-0.40), and CKD (0.14 eICU, 0.19 MargheritaTre).
claims.evidence: AODTrauma = -0.23 ... we AODSepsis = −0.27 and AODCancer = -0.38 ... AODage∈[18,39] = 0.21 ... AODAsian = −0.40 ... In the same cohort AODCKD = 0.14. In MargheritaTre (Suppl. Info S12 Figure) AODCKD = 0.19.

claims.claim: Class distribution in AmsterdamUMCdb was 88% transient AKI, 8.15% T72, 2.99% RRT24, 0.06% D48.
claims.evidence: The 88% of the AmsterdamUMCdb cohort has transient AKI, 8.15% has persistent AKI stage 3 due to primary endpoint T72, 2.99% has persistent AKI stage 3 due to RRT administration, while 0.06% is persistent due to death after prologued AKI stage 3.

claims.claim: Precision-recall metrics are preferred over ROC for imbalanced low-incidence prediction problems such as persistent AKI stage 3.
claims.evidence: in imbalanced problems the Precision Recall (PR) should be preferred [23]. The ROC curve, while useful, can be misleading in imbalanced datasets by resulting in high auROC values only due to the low incidence of the prediction endpoint.

claims.claim: The model cannot discriminate between AKI types (nephrotoxic, inflammatory, septic), a limitation shared with most prospective studies.
claims.evidence: Third limitation is the impossibility of discriminating between AKI types (nephrotoxic, inflammatory, versus septic). This limitation also affects most prospective studies [11].

claims.claim: Study population comprised 6,996 adults with incident HF (5,149 HFpEF and 1,847 HFrEF) from the Vanderbilt health system, 2008-2022.
claims.evidence: We identified 6,996 patients with incident HF (5,149 with HFpEF and 1,847 with HFrEF) (See Table 1).

claims.claim: AKI occurred in the ascertainment period in 6.9% of HFpEF patients and 5.7% of HFrEF patients.
claims.evidence: An AKI event occurred during the ascertainment period in 6.9% of those who developed HFpEF and 5.7% of those who developed HFrEF (see Table 2).

claims.claim: AKI severity distribution was higher among HFrEF (61/20/19% stages 1/2/3) than HFpEF (72/16/13%), not statistically significant.
claims.evidence: The overall distribution of AKI severity was higher among those who developed HFrEF (61%, 20%, and 19% for stages 1, 2, and 3, respectively) versus HFpEF (72%, 16%, and 13% for stages 1, 2, and 3, respectively, P = 0.062)

claims.claim: In unadjusted analysis AKI was not preferentially associated with HF subtype (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.65-1.02).
claims.evidence: In the unadjusted analysis, AKI was not preferentially associated with HF subtype (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.65 – 1.02).

claims.claim: Adjusted stage 1 AKI was associated with 32% higher odds of HFpEF (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.51-0.91).
claims.evidence: When examined by AKI severity, stage 1 AKI was associated with 32% higher odds of HFpEF (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.51 – 0.91) whereas stage 2–3 had a non-significant trend towards HFrEF (OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.76 – 1.63).

claims.claim: Models adjusted for 37 covariates ascertained prior to the AKI ascertainment window.
claims.evidence: To control for confounding, the models included 37 covariates which were ascertained prior to the AKI ascertainment window (see Fig. 2) and included demographics, baseline conditions, and medications.

claims.claim: Exposure creatinine data were drawn from hospitalization records 31-730 days before HF diagnosis to exclude AKI concurrent with acute HF.
claims.evidence: Exposure data (inpatient serum creatinine values) were obtained from hospitalization records 31 – 730 days prior to the outcome date. Exposure data was not captured in the 30 days prior to outcome date to exclude AKI that occurred concurrently with acute HF.

claims.claim: Among men, stage 1 AKI was associated with 45% higher odds of HFpEF (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38-0.81); sex-by-AKI interaction was not significant.
claims.evidence: Among men, AKI (all stages) was associated with 27% higher odds of HFpEF (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53 – 0.99). Stage 1 AKI was associated with 45% higher odds of HFpEF (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38 – 0.81)

claims.claim: Post hoc model found an additional severe AKI (stage 2-3) effect significantly associated with HFrEF (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.03-2.63).
claims.evidence: the additional severe AKI effect (stage 2–3 AKI) was associated with 64% higher odds of HFrEF which was statistically significant (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.03 – 2.63)

claims.claim: Of 460 patients with AKI, 39 had an MI during or within 5 days of the AKI hospitalization; 31 developed HFpEF and 8 HFrEF.
claims.evidence: Of the 460 patients with AKI, 39 had an MI (defined by presence of both a diagnosis code for myocardial infarction and elevated troponin level) during or within 5 days of the AKI hospitalization; of these, 31 developed HFpEF and 8 developed HFrEF.

claims.claim: Authors recommend close follow-up with attention to volume status and cardiac function after discharge even after mild AKI.
claims.evidence: Close follow-up with particular attention to volume status and cardiac function after discharge is warranted after even mild AKI.

claims.claim: Limitations include a predominantly White population and inclusion of only inpatient AKI, which may underestimate AKI events; causation cannot be inferred.
claims.evidence: Limitations include a predominantly White population, which may limit generalizability to more diverse populations, and inclusion of only inpatient AKI, which may underestimate number of AKI events.

claims.claim: For patients without an available outpatient baseline creatinine, the lowest creatinine during the AKI hospitalization was used as baseline.
claims.evidence: For those without an available baseline in the prior year, the low- est serum creatinine during the AKI hospitalization was used.

claims.claim: For patients with more than one AKI event during the ascertainment period, the most severe AKI was used.
claims.evidence: For patients with more than one AKI event during the ascertainment period, the most severe AKI was used in the analysis.

claims.claim: Trametinib is an FDA-approved selective MEK1/2 inhibitor evaluated for protection against cisplatin-induced AKI in mice.
claims.evidence: This study evaluated the protective effects of trametinib, an FDA-approved selective inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase 1/2 (MEK1/2), against cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury (AKI) in mice.

claims.claim: The experiment used four groups of eight mice: control, trametinib, cisplatin, and cisplatin plus trametinib.
claims.evidence: The experimental design included four groups, control, trametinib, cisplatin, and a combination of cisplatin and trametinib, each consisting of eight mice.

claims.claim: Cisplatin 20 mg/kg intraperitoneally induced kidney injury; trametinib 3 mg/kg was given by oral gavage daily for three days, with assessment 72 h after cisplatin.
claims.evidence: Cisplatin was administered intraperitoneally at a dose of 20 mg/kg to induce kidney injury, while trametinib was administered via oral gavage at 3 mg/kg daily for three days. Assessments were conducted 72 h after cisplatin administration.

claims.claim: Trametinib dosing started one hour after the cisplatin injection.
claims.evidence: The Tra and CP + Tra groups were orally administered trametinib [3 mg/kg body weight per day in 200 μL of 1% carboxymethylcullulose, 0.4% Tween80, and 5% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)] daily for three consecutive days, starting from one hour after the cisplatin injection.

claims.claim: Cisplatin increased serum creatinine and BUN, and trametinib significantly reduced both.
claims.evidence: trametinib treatment significantly mitigated the cisplatin-induced elevations in serum crea- tinine and BUN levels (creatinine: 1.78 ± 0.22 mg/dL versus 0.79 ± 0.12, p < 0.001; BUN: 153.1 ± 19.0 mg/dL versus 84.8 ± 10.8, p < 0.01; Figure 1C,D).

claims.claim: Trametinib alone did not change serum creatinine or BUN versus control mice.
claims.evidence: Additionally, treatment with trametinib alone did not result in significant differences in serum creatinine and BUN levels compared to the control mice (Figure 1C,D).

claims.claim: Tubular injury was scored 0-5 by percentage of damaged tubules in a blinded manner.
claims.evidence: Tubular injury was scored on a scale from 0 to 5 based on the percentage of damaged tubules: 0 for 0% damage, 1 for ≤10%, 2 for 11–25%, 3 for 26–50%, 4 for 51–75%, and 5 for 76–100%. This scoring was performed in a blinded manner [48].

claims.claim: Trametinib reduced tubular injury scores in cisplatin-injected mice from 2.63 to 1.13.
claims.evidence: treatment with trametinib resulted in a marked amelioration of these histopathological changes, which was quantitatively reflected in the substantially lower scores for tubular injury (2.63 ± 0.38 versus 1.13 ± 0.23, p < 0.001; Figure 2A,B).

claims.claim: Trametinib reduced KIM-1 positive area from 34.1% to 9.8% and reduced renal NGAL protein.
claims.evidence: trametinib treatment resulted in a significant reduction in KIM-1 expression, as evidenced by the reduced proportion of the area stained positively for KIM-1 (34.1 ± 3.7% versus 9.8 ± 1.3%, p < 0.001; Figure 3A,B).

claims.claim: Trametinib preserved proximal tubule brush border, increasing LTL-positive area from 5.9% to 16.8%.
claims.evidence: trametinib treatment resulted in a significant increase in the area with positive LTL staining in mice injected with cisplatin (5.9 ± 0.8% versus 16.8 ± 2.2%, p < 0.001; Figure 4A,B), indicating an effective preservation of the brush border structure.

claims.claim: Trametinib reduced serum TNF-alpha, IL-6 and IL-1 beta in cisplatin-injected mice.
claims.evidence: trametinib treatment lowered the serum levels of tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and IL-1β in cisplatin-injected mice (TNF-α: 107.3 ± 8.2 pg/mL versus 45.1 ± 5.6 pg/mL, p < 0.001;

claims.claim: Trametinib reversed cisplatin-induced NF-kappaB pathway activation in the kidney.
claims.evidence: we found that cisplatin injection elevated levels of p- IκBα, p-NF-κB p65, and NF-κB p65, while reducing IκBα levels (Figure 6A–C). However, these effects induced by cisplatin were significantly reversed when the mice were treated with trametinib

claims.claim: Trametinib lowered oxidative stress markers 4-HNE and MDA and restored the GSH/GSSG ratio.
claims.evidence: It also lowered lipid peroxidation by-products, restored the reduced glutathione/oxidized glutathione ratio, and downregulated NADPH oxidase 4.

claims.claim: Trametinib reduced TUNEL-positive apoptotic cells from 30.3 to 7.4 per field and lowered cleaved caspase-3, cleaved PARP-1, p53 and Bax.
claims.evidence: trametinib treatment significantly mitigated this effect, leading to a considerable decrease in the count of TUNEL-stained apoptotic cells in mice injected with cisplatin (30.3 ± 5.4 versus 7.4 ± 1.4, p < 0.001; Figure 8A,B).

claims.claim: Trametinib reduced RIPK1, RIPK3 and p-MLKL, indicating inhibition of necroptosis.
claims.evidence: trametinib treatment markedly reduced the ex- pression of these proteins (RIPK1: 10.51 ± 0.39 versus 1.78 ± 0.18, p < 0.001; RIPK3: 12.82 ± 0.63 versus 2.08 ± 0.28, p < 0.001; p-MLKL: 2.62 ± 0.31 versus 0.84 ± 0.06, p < 0.01; Figure 9A,B), suggesting that trametinib provides protection against necroptosis.

claims.claim: An earlier study by Brown et al. found trametinib did not improve AKI in a short-term high-dose cisplatin model, conflicting with this study.
claims.evidence: According to their findings, although trametinib increased survival rates, it did not improve AKI in a short-term, high-dose model of cisplatin-induced AKI.

claims.claim: The authors attribute the conflicting results to dose and route differences: 3 mg/kg oral versus 1 mg/kg intraperitoneal trametinib, and cisplatin 20 mg/kg versus 30 mg/kg.
claims.evidence: In our study, trametinib was administered at a dose of 3 mg/kg by oral gavage for three days post-cisplatin administration, while Brown et al. administered trametinib at a lower dose of 1 mg/kg by intraperitoneal injection for the same duration.

claims.claim: Real-world data document MEK inhibitor-associated AKI including trametinib, though characterized as rare and reversible.
claims.evidence: A recent real-world study has documented cases of AKI associated with the use of MEK inhibitors, including trametinib, and demonstrated their toxicity in human kidney-derived cell lines [23]. Despite these findings, researchers have concluded that AKI related to trametinib is rare and reversible [23].

claims.claim: Findings are limited by the mouse model and may not translate to human physiology.
claims.evidence: First, the use of a mouse model, while valuable for initial investigations, may not fully replicate complex human physiological responses to treatment. Consequently, the findings from this study should be cautiously interpreted when considering translational implications.

claims.claim: The high-dose short-term model does not replicate gradual clinical cisplatin nephrotoxicity; low-dose long-term studies are needed.
claims.evidence: However, this model does not fully replicate the gradual onset and progression of nephrotoxicity typically observed with the clinical use of cisplatin administered at lower doses over prolonged periods.

claims.claim: Sample size of 8 per group was determined by power analysis at 5% significance, 80% power and large effect size 0.7.
claims.evidence: The sample size (n = 8 per group) was determined based on calculations using G*Power software version 3.1.9.4 (Heinrich-Heine-Universität Düsseldorf, Düsseldorf, Germany), with a significance level of 5%, a minimum power of 80%, and a large effect size (0.7).

claims.claim: Group comparisons used one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests, significance at p < 0.05.
claims.evidence: Group comparisons were conducted using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) complemented by Bonfer- roni’s post hoc tests to discern statistical differences. Statistical significance was established at p values less than 0.05 for all analyses.

claims.claim: The 1-week or 48-hour timeframe applies to diagnosis of AKI, not to staging; a patient can be staged over the entire episode.
claims.evidence: Importantly, the 1-week or 48-hour timeframe is for diagnosis of AKI, not staging. A patient can be staged over the entire episode of AKI

claims.claim: There is no stipulation as to when the 1-week or 48-hour time periods occur; they need not be the first week or 48 hours of hospital or ICU stay.
claims.evidence: Importantly, there is no stipulation as to when the 1-week or 48-hour time periods can occur. It is stated unequivocally that it does not need to be the first week or 48 hours of a hospital or ICU stay.

claims.claim: A 50% SCr increase over 2 weeks does not fulfill AKI diagnostic criteria, even if it ultimately results in complete loss of kidney function.
claims.evidence: a disease process that results in a 50% increase in SCr over 2 weeks would not fulfill diagnostic criteria for AKI even if it ultimately resulted in complete loss of kidney function

claims.claim: In patients without CKD, a SCr obtained 6 months or even 1 year previously reasonably reflects premorbid baseline.
claims.evidence: it is reasonable in patients without CKD to assume that SCr will be stable over several months or even years, so that a SCr obtained 6 months or even 1 year previously would reasonable reflect the patient’s premorbid baseline

claims.claim: Diagnosis of AKI requires a second SCr value for comparison, either measured within 48 hours or a prior/estimated baseline.
claims.evidence: the diagnosis of AKI requires a second SCr value for comparison. This SCr could be a second measured SCr obtained within 48 hours, and if it is X0.3 mg/dl (X26.5 mmol/l) greater than the first SCr, AKI can be diagnosed.

claims.claim: The coefficient of variation for SCr by clinical testing methods is under 5%, but daily biological variation may be as great as 10%.
claims.evidence: While the coefficient of variation for SCr is very small (o5%) by various clinical testing methods ... Furthermore, daily variation in SCr due to differences in diet and activity may be as great as 10%.

claims.claim: SCr may be falsely lowered by large-volume fluid resuscitation or transfusion, so a normal value may not rule out AKI.
claims.evidence: the clinician should be cognizant of possibility that SCr may be falsely lowered by large-volume fluid resuscitation or transfusion; thus, a normal value may not rule out AKI

claims.claim: Not all patients with AKI meet the eGFR criteria for the definition of AKD.
claims.evidence: Not all patients with AKI would meet the eGFR criteria for the definition of AKD.

claims.claim: The GFR/SCr diagnostic algorithm uses three sequential questions to classify AKI, AKD and CKD.
claims.evidence: Figure 7 provides a diagnostic algorithm based on a sequential approach through three questions: i) Is GFR decreased or is SCr increased ...; ii) Is SCr increasing or GFR decreasing ...; and iii) Does the decrease in GFR or increase in SCr resolve within 3 months?

claims.claim: A normal GFR of ~125 ml/min corresponds to ~107 ml/kg/h for a 70-kg adult; urine volume <0.5 ml/kg/h would reflect reabsorption of more than 99.5% of glomerular filtrate.
claims.evidence: If GFR is normal (approximately 125 ml/min, corresponding to approximately 107 ml/kg/h for a 70-kg adult), then reduction in urine volume to o0.5 ml/kg/h would reflect reabsorption of more than 99.5% of glomerular filtrate.

claims.claim: If GFR and SCr are normal and stable over 24 hours, it is generally not necessary to measure urine flow rate to assess kidney function.
claims.evidence: if GFR and SCr are normal and stable over an interval of 24 hours, it is generally not necessary to measure urine flow rate in order to assess kidney function

claims.claim: Urine flow thresholds for the definition of AKI were derived empirically and are less well substantiated than SCr thresholds.
claims.evidence: the thresholds for urine flow for the definition of AKI have been derived empirically and are less well substantiated than the thresholds for increase in SCr

claims.claim: In 665 normal volunteers median renal length was 11.2 cm on the left and 10.9 cm on the right.
claims.evidence: In a study of 665 normal volunteers,69 median renal lengths were 11.2 cm on the left side and 10.9 cm on the right side.

claims.claim: In the VISEP study hypertonic 10% HES 200/0.5 caused a significantly higher rate of AKI than Ringer's lactate (34.9% vs 22.8%).
claims.evidence: the hypertonic HES group had a significantly higher rate of AKI (34.9% vs. 22.8%) and more days on which RRT was required

claims.claim: In the SAFE study patients in the albumin arm received 27% less study fluid than the saline arm (2247 vs 3096 ml).
claims.evidence: patients in the albumin arm received 27% less study fluid compared to the saline arm (2247 vs. 3096 ml) and were approximately 1 l less positive in overall fluid balance

claims.claim: In cardiac surgery patients, 10% 250/0.45 HES showed no evidence of nephrotoxicity versus saline (AKI by RIFLE 16% in both groups, RRT 1% in each).
claims.evidence: the study found no evidence of nephrotoxicity: no difference in the daily creatinine, deve- lopment of AKI by RIFLE criteria during hospital stay (16% in both groups), or need for RRT (1% in each group)

claims.claim: Preservation of renal perfusion in vasomotor paralysis can only be achieved with systemic vasopressors once intravascular volume has been restored.
claims.evidence: In the setting of vasomotor paralysis, preservation or improvement of renal perfusion can only be achieved through use of systemic vasopressors once intravascular volume has been restored.105

claims.claim: It is not known which vasopressor agent is most effective for prevention or treatment of AKI with septic shock.
claims.evidence: It is not known which vasopressor agent is most effective for prevention or treatment of patients with AKI and septic shock.

claims.claim: KDIGO defines AKI by any of three criteria: SCr rise >=0.3 mg/dl within 48 h, SCr >=1.5 times baseline within prior 7 days, or urine volume <0.5 ml/kg/h for 6 hours.
claims.evidence: 2.1.1: AKI is defined as any of the following (Not Graded): K Increase in SCr by X0.3 mg/dl (X26.5 lmol/l) within 48 hours; or K Increase in SCr to X1.5 times baseline, which is known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days; or K Urine volume o0.5 ml/kg/h for 6 hours.

claims.claim: The cause of AKI should be determined whenever possible (ungraded).
claims.evidence: 2.1.3: The cause of AKI should be determined whenever possible. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: Patients should be staged according to the criterion (creatinine or urine output) that gives the highest stage.
claims.evidence: For staging purposes, patients should be staged accord- ing to the criteria that give them the highest stage. Thus when creatinine and urine output map to different stages, ... the patient is staged according to the highest (worst) stage.

claims.claim: Stage 3 by SCr >4.0 mg/dl now requires the patient to first meet the AKI definition rather than an unspecified acute rise of >=0.5 mg/dl.
claims.evidence: For patients reaching Stage 3 by SCr 44.0 mg/dl (4354 mmol/l), rather than require an acute increase of X0.5 mg/dl (X44 mmol/l) over an unspecified time period, we instead require that the patient first achieve the creatinine- based change specified in the definition

claims.claim: Kidney failure is defined as GFR <15 ml/min per 1.73 m2 or requirement for RRT.
claims.evidence: Kidney failure is defined as a GFR o15 ml/min per 1.73 m2 body surface area, or requirement for RRT, although it is recognized that RRT may be required earlier in the evolution of AKI.

claims.claim: RIFLE and AKIN criteria identify overlapping but different patient sets: RIFLE missed 9% of AKIN-detected cases, AKIN missed 26.9% of RIFLE-detected cases.
claims.evidence: The original RIFLE criteria failed to detect 9% of cases that were detected by AKIN criteria. However, the AKIN criteria missed 26.9% of cases detected by RIFLE.

claims.claim: Cases missed by RIFLE but classified as AKIN Stage 1 had hospital mortality nearly twice that of patients with no AKI by either criteria (25% vs 13%).
claims.evidence: However, cases missed by RIFLE but identified as Stage 1 by AKIN also had hospital mortality rates nearly twice that of patients who had no evidence of AKI by either criteria (25% vs. 13%).

claims.claim: In Uchino et al., RIFLE class was an independent predictor of hospital mortality with odds ratios of 2.5 (R), 5.4 (I), and 10.1 (F).
claims.evidence: They found that class R carried an odds ratio of hospital mortality of 2.5, I of 5.4, and F of 10.1.

claims.claim: Thakar et al. reported odds ratios for hospital mortality of 2.2 for Stage 1, 6.1 for Stage 2, and 8.6 for Stage 3.
claims.evidence: Patients with Stage 1 (X0.3 mg/dl or X26.5 mmol/l) increase in SCr but less than a two-fold increase had an odds ratio of 2.2; with Stage 2 (corresponding to RIFLE-I), there was an odds ratio of 6.1; and in Stage 3 (RIFLE-F), an odds ratio of 8.6 for hospital mortality was calculated.

claims.claim: In Hoste et al., only 14% of patients reaching RIFLE 'F' received RRT, yet their hospital mortality was more than five times that of ICU patients without AKI.
claims.evidence: In a study by Hoste et al.,2 only 14% of patients reaching RIFLE ‘‘F’’ received RRT, yet these patients experienced a hospital mortality rate more than five times that of the same ICU population without AKI.

claims.claim: Incidence of AKI in Northern Scotland was 2147 per million population, with sepsis a precipitating factor in 47% of patients.
claims.evidence: The incidence of AKI was 2147 per million population.31 Sepsis was a precipitating factor in 47% of patients.

claims.claim: Depending on the definition used, ARF has been reported to affect 1% to 25% of ICU patients with mortality rates from 15-60%.
claims.evidence: Depending on the definition used, ARF has been reported to affect from 1% to 25% of ICU patients and has lead to mortality rates from 15–60%.

claims.claim: A survey found at least 35 different definitions of acute renal failure in the literature.
claims.evidence: A recent survey revealed the use of at least 35 definitions in the literature.19

claims.claim: Roughly a third of AKI cases are community-acquired and may be missed by limiting analysis to documented SCr increases.
claims.evidence: Preliminary data from a 20 000-patient database from the University of Pittsburgh suggests that roughly a third of AKI cases are community-acquired33 and many cases may be missed by limiting analysis to documented increases in SCr.

claims.claim: Nonoliguric renal failure occurs because injured tubules lose maximal concentrating ability so urine volume may be normal.
claims.evidence: Conversely, when the tubules are injured, maximal concentrating ability is impaired and urine volume may even be normal (i.e., nonoliguric renal failure).

claims.claim: High urine osmolality with low urine sodium in oliguria and azotemia indicates intact tubular function but should not be interpreted as benign or prerenal azotemia.
claims.evidence: a high urine osmolality coupled with a low urine sodium in the face of oliguria and azotemia is strong evidence of intact tubular function. However, this should not be interpreted as ‘‘benign’’ or even prerenal azotemia.

claims.claim: The term ATN describes a clinical situation with adequate renal perfusion to maintain tubular integrity but not sustain glomerular filtration.
claims.evidence: the term ATN is used to describe a clinical situation in which there is adequate renal perfusion to largely maintain tubular integrity, but not ... to sustain glomerular filtration.

claims.claim: KDIGO recommendations 2.1.1 and 2.1.2 represent the combination of RIFLE and AKIN criteria.
claims.evidence: Recommendations 2.1.1 and 2.1.2 represent the combination of RIFLE and AKIN criteria (Table 3).

claims.claim: Guideline recommendations are graded level 1 ('We recommend') or level 2 ('We suggest'), with evidence quality A (high) to D (very low) per GRADE.
claims.evidence: The strength of each recom- mendation is rated as level 1 which means ‘‘strong’’ or level 2 which means ‘‘weak’’ or discretionary. ... each statement is assigned a grade for the quality of the supporting evidence, A (high), B (moderate), C (low), or D (very low).

claims.claim: Diagnosis and staging of AKI statements are ungraded, based on unanimous Work Group consensus, and should not be viewed as weaker than graded recommendations.
claims.evidence: Some of our most important guideline topics involve diagnosis and staging or AKI, and here the Work Group chose to provide ungraded statements. ... they should not be viewed as weaker than graded recommendations.

claims.claim: Guideline development screened 18 385 citations across four topic areas: definition/classification, prevention, pharmacologic treatment, and RRT.
claims.evidence: The four major topic areas of interest for AKI included: i) definition and classification; ii) prevention; iii) pharmacologic treatment; and iv) RRT. ... Overall, we screened 18 385 citations.

claims.claim: Studies on AKI from rhabdomyolysis, specific infections, and poisoning or drug overdose were excluded from the evidence review.
claims.evidence: We excluded studies on AKI from rhabdomyolysis, specific infections, and poisoning or drug overdose.

claims.claim: The Stage 3 SCr >4.0 mg/dl threshold is problematic for small pediatric patients with low muscle mass, prompting the pediatric-modified RIFLE criteria based on estimated creatinine clearance.
claims.evidence: This is problematic for smaller pediatric patients, including infants and children with low muscle mass who may not be able to achieve a SCr of 4.0 mg/dl (354 mmol/l). Thus, the pediatric- modified RIFLE AKI criteria32 were developed using a change in estimated creatinine clearance (eCrCl)

claims.claim: Creatinine criteria should be used along with urine output for diagnosis and staging because published RIFLE GFR changes do not correspond precisely to SCr changes.
claims.evidence: The changes in GFR that were published with the original RIFLE criteria do not correspond precisely to changes in SCr. As SCr is measured and GFR can only be estimated, creatinine criteria should be used along with urine output for the diagnosis (and staging) of AKI.

claims.claim: KDIGO defines AKI as an increase in SCr of at least 0.3 mg/dl within 48 hours, an increase to at least 1.5 times baseline within the prior 7 days, or urine volume below 0.5 ml/kg/h for 6 hours.
claims.evidence: 2.1.1: AKI is defined as any of the following (Not Graded): K Increase in SCr by X0.3 mg/dl (X26.5 lmol/l) within 48 hours; or K Increase in SCr to X1.5 times baseline, which is known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days; or K Urine volume o0.5 ml/kg/h for 6 hours.

claims.claim: AKI stage 3 includes eGFR decrease to below 35 ml/min per 1.73 m2 in patients under 18 years.
claims.evidence: OR, In patients o18 years, decrease in eGFR to o35 ml/min per 1.73 m2 o0.3 ml/kg/h for X24 hours OR Anuria for X12 hours

claims.claim: The cause of AKI should be determined whenever possible.
claims.evidence: 2.1.3: The cause of AKI should be determined whenever possible. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: Patients at increased risk for AKI should be tested with SCr and urine output measurements, with frequency and duration individualized.
claims.evidence: 2.2.3: Test patients at increased risk for AKI with measurements of SCr and urine output to detect AKI. (Not Graded) Individualize frequency and duration of monitoring based on patient risk and clinical course. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: Patients should be evaluated 3 months after AKI for resolution, new onset, or worsening of pre-existing CKD.
claims.evidence: 2.3.4: Evaluate patients 3 months after AKI for resolution, new onset, or worsening of pre-existing CKD. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: KDIGO recommends against low-dose dopamine to prevent or treat AKI (1A).
claims.evidence: 3.5.1: We recommend not using low-dose dopamine to prevent or treat AKI. (1A)

claims.claim: KDIGO recommends iso-osmolar or low-osmolar rather than high-osmolar iodinated contrast media in patients at increased risk of CI-AKI (1B).
claims.evidence: 4.3.2: We recommend using either iso-osmolar or low-osmolar iodinated contrast media, rather than high-osmolar iodinated contrast media in patients at increased risk of CI-AKI. (1B)

claims.claim: KDIGO recommends against using oral fluids alone in patients at increased risk of CI-AKI (1C).
claims.evidence: 4.4.2: We recommend not using oral fluids alone in patients at increased risk of CI-AKI. (1C)

claims.claim: The decision to start RRT should consider the broader clinical context and trends rather than single BUN and creatinine thresholds alone.
claims.evidence: 5.1.2: Consider the broader clinical context, the presence of conditions that can be modified with RRT, and trends of laboratory tests—rather than single BUN and creatinine thresholds alone—when making the decision to start RRT. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: Preferred vein order for dialysis catheter insertion is right jugular, femoral, left jugular, then subclavian.
claims.evidence: K First choice: right jugular vein; K Second choice: femoral vein; K Third choice: left jugular vein; K Last choice: subclavian vein with preference for the dominant side.

claims.claim: The guideline used the GRADE approach to appraise evidence quality and recommendation strength.
claims.evidence: Appraisal of the quality of the evidence and the strength of recommendations followed the GRADE approach.

claims.claim: Only 11 (18%) of recommendations had overall quality of evidence graded 'A'.
claims.evidence: In all, there were only 11 (18%) recommendations in this guideline for which the overall quality of evidence was graded ‘A,’ whereas 20 (32.8%) were graded ‘B,’ 23 (37.7%) were graded ‘C,’ and 7 (11.5%) were graded ‘D.’

claims.claim: The creatinine conversion factor from mg/dl to µmol/l is 88.4.
claims.evidence: Creatinine (serum) mg/dl 88.4 mmol/l

claims.claim: The guideline is based on the best information available as of February 2011.
claims.evidence: This Clinical Practice Guideline document is based upon the best information available as of February 2011.

claims.claim: In pRIFLE, patients automatically reach Stage 3 if eCrCl falls below 35 ml/min per 1.73 m2.
claims.evidence: In pRIFLE, patients automatically reach Stage 3 if they develop an eCrCl o35 ml/min per 1.73 m2.

claims.claim: The SCr-change-based AKI definition, including a 0.3 mg/dl increase, applies to pediatric patients.
claims.evidence: the SCr change based AKI definition (recommendation 2.1.1) is applicable to pediatric patients, including an increase of 0.3 mg/dl (26.5 mmol/l) SCr.32

claims.claim: For both AKIN stage and RIFLE criteria, only one criterion (creatinine rise or urine output decline) needs to be fulfilled, and class is based on the worst of either GFR or urine output criteria.
claims.evidence: For both AKIN stage and RIFLE criteria, only one criterion (creatinine rise or urine output decline) needs to be fulfilled. Class is based on the worst of either GFR or urine output criteria.

claims.claim: Creatinine in SI units is converted to mg/dl by dividing by 88.4.
claims.evidence: Note: For conversion of creatinine expressed in SI units to mg/dl, divide by 88.4.

claims.claim: Urine output criteria for AKI are less well validated and may misclassify very obese patients with normal urine output.
claims.evidence: For very obese patients, urine output criteria for AKI may include some patients with normal urine output.

claims.claim: Clinical judgment regarding drugs such as ACE inhibitors, fluid balance and other factors must be included when applying urine output criteria.
claims.evidence: in individual patients the need for clinical judgment regarding the effects of drugs (e.g., angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors [ACE-I]), fluid balance, and other factors must be included

claims.claim: Risk of AKI is determined by the interaction between susceptibility factors and the type and extent of exposure to insults.
claims.evidence: It is the interaction between susceptibility and the type and extent of exposure to insults that determines the risk of occurrence of AKI.

claims.claim: Approximately 30% of patients who recover from AKI remain at increased risk of CKD, cardiovascular disease, and death.
claims.evidence: the fact that some 30% of patients who recover from AKI remain at increased risk of CKD, cardiovascular disease, and death calls for the identification of the risk factors

claims.claim: High-risk inpatients should have SCr measured at least daily and more frequently after an exposure; critically ill patients should have urine output monitoring.
claims.evidence: as a general rule, high risk in-patients should have SCr measured at least daily and more frequently after an exposure, and critically ill patients should have urine output monitoring.

claims.claim: A UK clinical practice assessment found only 50% of AKI patients received a 'good' overall standard of care, falling to just over 30% for hospital-acquired AKI.
claims.evidence: only 50% of patients with AKI were considered to have received a ''good'' overall standard of care. This figure fell to ... just over 30% if AKI developed during a hospital admission rather than being diagnosed before admission.53

claims.claim: There was unacceptable delay in recognizing AKI in 43% of patients developing AKI after admission, and in a fifth its development was predictable and avoidable.
claims.evidence: there was an unacceptable delay in recognizing AKI in 43% of those that developed the condition after admission, and that in a fifth of such patients its develop- ment was predictable and avoidable.

claims.claim: Nephrotoxic drugs account for some part of AKI in 20-30% of patients.
claims.evidence: Nephrotoxic drugs account for some part of AKI in 20–30% of patients.

claims.claim: As many as two-thirds of all cases of AKI begin prior to hospitalization (community-acquired AKI).
claims.evidence: as many as two-thirds of all cases of AKI begin prior to hospitali- zation (community-acquired AKI).

claims.claim: Excluding hemodilution from massive fluid resuscitation, the lowest SCr obtained during hospitalization is usually equal to or greater than baseline and should be used to diagnose and stage AKI.
claims.evidence: excluding some cases of hemo- dilution secondary to massive fluid resuscitation (discussed below), the lowest SCr obtained during a hospitalization is usually equal to or greater than the baseline. This SCr should be used to diagnose (and stage) AKI.

claims.claim: Estimating baseline SCr risks labeling a patient with AKI when the true diagnosis was unidentified CKD.
claims.evidence: many cases of CKD are not identified, and thus estimating the baseline SCr may risk labeling a patient with AKI when in reality the diagnosis was unidentified CKD.

claims.claim: Estimated baseline SCr for a 70-year-old white female is 0.8 mg/dl (71 umol/l), while for a 20-year-old black male it is 1.5 mg/dl (133 umol/l).
claims.evidence: If Case A were a 70-year-old white female with no evidence or history of CKD, the baseline SCr would be 0.8 mg/dl (71 mmol/l) ... if the patient was a 20-year-old black male, his baseline SCr would be estimated at 1.5 mg/dl (133 mmol/l).

claims.claim: Static hemodynamic variables like central venous pressure are less useful than dynamic variables such as pulse-pressure variation and IVC filling.
claims.evidence: Static variables like central venous pressure are not nearly as useful as dynamic variables, such as pulse-pressure variation, inferior vena cava filling by ultrasound and echocardio- graphic appearance of the heart

claims.claim: Studies using both SCr and urine output to diagnose AKI show increased incidence, suggesting SCr alone may miss many patients.
claims.evidence: studies using both SCr and urine output to diagnose AKI show increased incidence, suggesting that the use of SCr alone may miss many patients.

claims.claim: AKI stage correlates with short-term and longer-term outcomes, so management should be tailored to stage.
claims.evidence: Because the stage of AKI has clearly been shown to correlate with short-term2,5,27,29 and even longer-term out- comes,31 it is advisable to tailor management to AKI stage.

claims.claim: Patients with AKI but without CKD at 3 months should be considered at increased risk for CKD and managed per KDOQI CKD Guideline 3.
claims.evidence: If patients do not have CKD, consider them to be at increased risk for CKD and care for them as detailed in the KDOQI CKD Guideline 3 for patients at increased risk for CKD.

claims.claim: Risk assessment in community-acquired AKI differs from hospital-acquired AKI because evidence derives from hospital data and opportunity to intervene before exposure is limited.
claims.evidence: Risk assessment in community-acquired AKI is different from hospital-acquired AKI, for two main reasons: i) Available evidence on risk factors is largely derived from hospital data and extrapolation to the community setting is questionable. ii) The opportunity to intervene, prior to exposure, is quite limited.

claims.claim: A large RCT found no significant difference in renal function or mortality between dopamine and norepinephrine as initial vasopressor in shock, but more arrhythmic events with dopamine.
claims.evidence: A large RCT109 comparing dopamine to norepinephrine as initial vasopres- sor in patients with shock showed no significant differences between groups with regard to renal function or mortality. However, there were more arrhythmic events among the patients treated with dopamine

claims.claim: Vasopressin increases blood pressure and diuresis compared to norepinephrine but is unproven for survival or reducing RRT need.
claims.evidence: Compared to nor- epinephrine, it increases blood pressure and enhances dieresis, but has not as yet been proven to enhance survival nor to reduce the need for RRT.

claims.claim: Mortality in RIFLE-R patients was 30.8% with vasopressin vs 54.7% with norepinephrine (P=0.01), not significant on multivariable analysis.
claims.evidence: Mortality rates in the R category patients treated with vasopressin compared to norepinephrine were 30.8 vs. 54.7%, P ¼ 0.01, but this did not reach significance in a multiple logistic regression analysis.

claims.claim: The Work Group concluded current data are insufficient to declare one vasoactive agent superior for preventing AKI, and such agents should not be withheld in vasomotor shock.
claims.evidence: The Work Group concluded that current clinical data are insufficient to conclude that one vasoactive agent is superior to another in preventing AKI, but emphasized that vasoactive agents should not be withheld from patients with vasomotor shock over concern for kidney perfusion.

claims.claim: KDIGO 3.1.3 suggests protocol-based hemodynamic and oxygenation management to prevent development or worsening of AKI in high-risk perioperative patients or septic shock (2C).
claims.evidence: 3.1.3: We suggest using protocol-based management of hemodynamic and oxygenation parameters to prevent development or worsening of AKI in high-risk patients in the perioperative setting (2C) or in patients with septic shock (2C).

claims.claim: EGDT targets within 6 hours: MAP >=65 mm Hg, CVP 8-12 mm Hg, improving lactate, ScvO2 >70%, and urine output >=0.5 ml/kg/h.
claims.evidence: The physiologic goals are: i) return of mean arterial blood pressure to X65 mm Hg; ii) central venous pressure between 8–12 mm Hg; iii) improvement in blood lactate levels; iv) central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) 470%; and v) a urine output of X0.5 ml/kg/h.

claims.claim: High-risk surgical patients include age >60 years, emergent surgery, elevated ASA score, and preoperative comorbid illnesses.
claims.evidence: reduce the risk of AKI following major surgical procedures in high-risk patients (e.g., age 460 years, emergent surgery, elevated American Society of Anesthesiologists score, preoperative comorbid illnesses)

claims.claim: KDIGO 3.3.1 suggests insulin therapy targeting plasma glucose 110-149 mg/dl (6.1-8.3 mmol/l) in critically ill patients (2C).
claims.evidence: 3.3.1: In critically ill patients, we suggest insulin therapy targeting plasma glucose 110–149 mg/dl (6.1–8.3 mmol/l). (2C)

claims.claim: In the surgical ICU Leuven trial, severe AKI (peak SCr >2.5 mg/dl) occurred in 7.2% with intensive insulin vs 11.2% with conventional insulin (P=0.04), and RRT in 4.8% vs 8.2% (P=0.007).
claims.evidence: severe AKI (peak SCr 42.5 mg/dl [4221 mmol/l]) developed in 7.2% of the IIT group, compared to 11.2% of the CIT group (P ¼ 0.04); the incidence of RRT was also lower in the IIT group than the CIT group (4.8% vs. 8.2%, respectively; P ¼ 0.007)

claims.claim: NICE-SUGAR found intensive glucose control (81-108 mg/dl) increased 90-day mortality vs conventional target <=180 mg/dl (OR 1.14; 95% CI 1.02-1.28; P=0.02) with no difference in new RRT (15.4% vs 14.5%).
claims.evidence: A total of 829 patients (27.5%) in the intensive-control group and 751 (24.9%) in the conventional-control group died (OR for intensive control, 1.14; 95% CI 1.02–1.28; P ¼ 0.02)... There was no significant difference between the two treatment groups in incidence of new RRT (15.4% vs. 14.5%)

claims.claim: Wiener meta-analysis of 29 RCTs (8432 patients) found no mortality difference (pooled RR 0.93) but a pooled RR of 5.13 for hypoglycemia <40 mg/dl with intensive insulin therapy.
claims.evidence: Twenty-seven studies reported no difference in hospital mortality (21.6% in IIT vs 23.3% in CIT) with a pooled RR of 0.93 (95% CI 0.85–1.03; P ¼ NS)... a pooled RR of 5.13 (95% CI 4.09–6.43; Po0.05)

claims.claim: KDIGO 3.3.2 suggests a total energy intake of 20-30 kcal/kg/d in patients with any stage of AKI (2C).
claims.evidence: 3.3.2: We suggest achieving a total energy intake of 20–30 kcal/kg/d in patients with any stage of AKI. (2C)

claims.claim: Energy provision should comprise 3-5 (maximum 7) g/kg carbohydrates and 0.8-1.0 g/kg fat.
claims.evidence: Energy provision should be composed of 3–5 (maximum 7) g per kilogram body weight carbohydrates and 0.8–1.0 g per kilogram body weight fat.

claims.claim: KDIGO 3.3.3 suggests avoiding protein restriction aimed at preventing or delaying initiation of RRT (2D).
claims.evidence: 3.3.3: We suggest to avoid restriction of protein intake with the aim of preventing or delaying initiation of RRT. (2D)

claims.claim: KDIGO 3.3.4 suggests protein 0.8-1.0 g/kg/d in noncatabolic AKI without dialysis, 1.0-1.5 g/kg/d on RRT, and up to 1.7 g/kg/d on CRRT or in hypercatabolic patients (2D).
claims.evidence: 3.3.4: We suggest administering 0.8–1.0 g/kg/d of protein in noncatabolic AKI patients without need for dialysis (2D), 1.0–1.5 g/kg/d in patients with AKI on RRT (2D), and up to a maximum of 1.7 g/kg/d in patients on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and in hypercatabolic patients. (2D)

claims.claim: In CRRT about 0.2 g amino acids are lost per liter of filtrate, totalling 10-15 g daily, plus 5-10 g of protein per day.
claims.evidence: In CRRT, about 0.2 g amino acids are lost per liter of filtrate, amounting to a total daily loss of 10–15 g amino acids. In addition, 5–10 g of protein are lost per day

claims.claim: KDIGO 3.3.5 suggests providing nutrition preferentially via the enteral route in patients with AKI (2C).
claims.evidence: 3.3.5: We suggest providing nutrition preferentially via the enteral route in patients with AKI. (2C)

claims.claim: If oral feeding is not possible, tube feeding should be initiated within 24 hours.
claims.evidence: If oral feeding is not possible, then enteral feeding (tube feeding) should be initiated within 24 hours, and has been shown to be safe and effective.

claims.claim: In 300 prospectively studied AKI patients, 42% presented with signs of severe malnutrition on admission.
claims.evidence: In a prospective study of 300 AKI patients, 42% presented with signs of severe malnutrition on admission.

claims.claim: Critically ill children should receive 100-130% of basal energy expenditure, estimable by the Caldwell-Kennedy equation.
claims.evidence: critically ill children, like adults, should receive 100–130% of the basal energy expenditure, which can be estimated with acceptable precision and accuracy by the Caldwell-Kennedy equation179: (resting energy expenditure [kcal/kg/d] ¼ 22 þ 31.05  weight [kg] þ 1.16  age [years])

claims.claim: In children with AKI on CRRT, maximal calorie prescription averaged 53, 31 and 21 kcal/kg/d and protein 2.4, 1.9 and 1.3 g/kg/d for ages <1, 1-13 and >13 years.
claims.evidence: the maximal calorie prescription in the course of treatment averaged 53, 31, and 21 kcal/kg/d, and that for protein intake 2.4, 1.9, and 1.3 g/kg/d in children aged o1, 1–13, and 413 years, respectively

claims.claim: KDIGO 3.4.1 recommends not using diuretics to prevent AKI (1B).
claims.evidence: 3.4.1: We recommend not using diuretics to prevent AKI. (1B)

claims.claim: KDIGO 3.4.2 suggests not using diuretics to treat AKI except in the management of volume overload (2C).
claims.evidence: 3.4.2: We suggest not using diuretics to treat AKI, except in the management of volume overload. (2C)

claims.claim: Observational studies showed 59-70% of AKI patients received diuretics at nephrology consultation or before starting RRT.
claims.evidence: Recent observational studies showed that 59–70% of patients with AKI were given diuretics at the time of nephrology consultation or before the start of RRT.

claims.claim: Systematic reviews found furosemide had no significant effect on in-hospital mortality, need for RRT, number of dialysis sessions, or persistent oliguria.
claims.evidence: Furosemide had no significant effect on in-hospital mortality, risk for requiring RRT, number of dialysis sessions, or even the proportion of patients with persistent oliguria.

claims.claim: Pooled analysis of prevention trials found no benefit of furosemide vs placebo for RRT incidence (RR 4.08).
claims.evidence: All three studies reported RRT incidence in patients randomized to furosemide (n ¼ 128) vs. placebo (n ¼ 127), with a pooled RR of 4.08 (95% CI 0.46–35.96; P ¼ 0.21).

claims.claim: Six studies of furosemide to treat AKI (600–3400 mg/d) showed no significant reduction in in-hospital mortality or RRT requirement.
claims.evidence: also included six studies that used furosemide to treat AKI, with doses ranging from 600 to 3400 mg/d (Figure 9 and Figure 10).192 No significant reduction was found for in-hospital mortality or for RRT requirement.

claims.claim: In 338 dialysis-requiring AKI patients, furosemide shortened time to 2 l/d diuresis but did not improve survival or reduce dialysis sessions.
claims.evidence: Although time to reach 2 l/d of diuresis was shorter with furosemide (5.7 days) than placebo (7.8 days, P ¼ 0.004), there was no difference in survival and number of dialysis sessions.

claims.claim: Continuous furosemide infusion at 0.5 mg/kg/hour was not associated with ototoxicity.
claims.evidence: When administered as continuous infusion a dose of 0.5 mg/kg/ hour was not associated with ototoxicity.195

claims.claim: Dopamine, mannitol and atrial natriuretic peptide increased renal dysfunction in diabetic patients receiving contrast media compared with saline alone.
claims.evidence: Dopamine, mannitol, and atrial natriuretic peptide were associated with a much higher incidence of renal dysfunction in diabetic subjects compared to patients receiving saline alone.

claims.claim: Low-dose dopamine (1–3 ug/kg/min) causes renal vasodilation, natriuresis and increased GFR in healthy individuals.
claims.evidence: Low-dose dopamine administration (1–3 mg/kg/min) to healthy individuals causes renal vasodila- tion, natriuresis, and increased GFR

claims.claim: Dopamine significantly increased renal vascular resistance in patients with AKI, unlike in healthy populations.
claims.evidence: Using Doppler ultrasound, Lauschke et al.209 found that dopamine signi- ficantly increased renal vascular resistance in AKI patients.

claims.claim: Meta-analysis of 61 trials of low-dose dopamine found no improvement in survival, dialysis requirement, or renal function.
claims.evidence: The authors analyzed 61 randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials of low-dose dopamine, and found no improvement of survival (Figure 11), no decrease in dialysis requirement (Figure 12), no improvement in renal function

claims.claim: Low-dose dopamine can trigger tachyarrhythmias and myocardial ischemia, decrease intestinal blood flow, cause hypopituitarism, and suppress T-cell function.
claims.evidence: It can trigger tachyarrhythmias and myocardial ischemia, decrease intestinal blood flow, cause hypopituitarism, and suppress T-cell function.208

claims.claim: Fenoldopam is a pure dopamine type-1 receptor agonist with renal hemodynamic effects similar to low-dose dopamine without systemic adrenergic stimulation.
claims.evidence: Fenoldopam mesylate is a pure dopamine type-1 receptor agonist that has similar hemodynamic renal effects as low-dose dopamine, without systemic a- or b-adrenergic stimulation.213

claims.claim: In a randomized trial, 24-hour fenoldopam infusion 0.1 ug/kg/min reduced AKI (12.6% vs 27.6%) and RRT (0% vs 8.2%) after high-risk cardiac surgery.
claims.evidence: AKI developed in 12 of 95 (12.6%) patients receiving fenoldopam and in 27 of 98 (27.6%) patients receiving placebo (P ¼ 0.02), and RRT was started in 0 of 95 and 8 of 98 (8.2%) patients, respectively (P ¼ 0.004).

claims.claim: Pooled analysis of three prophylactic fenoldopam trials showed no reduction in AKI incidence (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.76–1.2).
claims.evidence: reported AKI incidence in patients randomized to fenoldo- pam (n ¼ 1790) vs. placebo (n ¼ 1839). The pooled RR and 95% CI was 0.96 (0.76–1.2), P ¼ NS.

claims.claim: Fenoldopam was ultimately found ineffective for prevention of contrast-induced AKI.
claims.evidence: despite promising pilot study findings, fenoldo- pam was ultimately found to be ineffective for the prevention of CI-AKI,220

claims.claim: In 504 critically ill AKI patients, 24-hour ANP infusion (0.2 ug/kg/min) had no effect on 21-day dialysis-free survival, mortality or creatinine.
claims.evidence: Despite the large size of the trial, ANP administration had no effect on 21-day dialysis-free survival, mortality, or change in plasma creatinine concentration.

claims.claim: Hypotension occurred more frequently with ANP in both large trials (46% vs 18% and 97% vs 58%).
claims.evidence: hypotension (systolic blood pressure o90 mm Hg) occurred more frequently in the ANP groups of both trials (in the first study, 46% vs. 18%, Po0.001; and in the second study, 97% vs. 58%, Po0.001)

claims.claim: In post-cardiac surgery AKI, ANP reduced 21-day dialysis rates from 47% to 21% (HR 0.28).
claims.evidence: Using prespecified dialysis criteria, 21% of patients in the ANP group and 47% in the placebo group were dialyzed within 21 days (hazard ratio [HR] 0.28; 95% CI 0.10–0.73; P ¼ 0.009).

claims.claim: ANP infusion increased GFR, filtration fraction, sodium excretion and renal oxygen consumption, whereas furosemide lowered GFR by 12% and renal oxygen consumption by 23%.
claims.evidence: Furosemide also lowered GFR by 12% and filtration fraction by 7%. Thus, although the balance of renal hemodynamic and tubular effects of the two drugs appears to favor furosemide for improving renal oxygen delivery-consumption balance, ANP is more likely to acutely improve GFR.

claims.claim: Pooled analysis of eight ANP treatment studies showed no difference in RRT requirement (OR 0.59) or mortality (OR 1.01).
claims.evidence: did not show significant difference for RRT requirement between the ANP and control groups (OR 0.59; 95% CI 0.32–1.08; P ¼ 0.12). There was also no significant difference for mortality (OR 1.01; 95% CI 0.72–1.43; P ¼ 0.89).

claims.claim: In cardiac surgery patients with LV dysfunction, nesiritide 0.01 ug/kg/min improved perioperative renal end-points versus placebo.
claims.evidence: Perioperative renal function quantified by the three renal primary end-points was better in the nesiritide group (peak SCr increase of 0.15 mg/dl [13.3 mmol/l] vs. placebo group 0.34 mg/dl [30.1 mmol/l]; Po0.001

claims.claim: The Nesiritide Study found no benefit for 21-day dialysis and/or death but reduced immediate postoperative AKIN-defined AKI (6.6% vs 28.5%).
claims.evidence: the study did demonstrate that the prophylactic use of nesiritide was associated with reduced incidence of AKI, the latter defined by the AKIN Group, in the immediate postoperative period (nesiritide 6.6% vs. placebo 28.5%, P ¼ 0.004)

claims.claim: The Work Group's recommendation against fenoldopam values avoiding hypotension over unproven benefit from low-quality single-center trials.
claims.evidence: The guideline recommendation against using fenoldopam places a high value on avoiding potential hypotension and harm associated with the use of this vasodilator in high-risk perioperative and ICU patients, and a low value on potential benefit

claims.claim: Further study is required to clarify the safety of loop diuretics in management of AKI patients.
claims.evidence: further study is required to clarify the safety of loop diuretics in the management of patients with AKI.

claims.claim: The Work Group suggests ANP, BNP, and nesiritide not be used for prevention or treatment of AKI because no definitive trials support their use.
claims.evidence: there are no definitive trials to support the use of ANP, BNP, or nesiritide for these purposes. Thus, the Work Group suggests that these agents not be used for prevention or treatment of AKI.

claims.claim: KDIGO research recommendation: further trials of ANP at doses below 0.1 mg/kg/min (0.01-0.05 mg/kg/min) for prevention or treatment of AKI.
claims.evidence: We recommend further trials of ANP at doses below 0.1 mg/kg/min, for the prevention or treatment of AKI. There is a possibility that ANP might be effective if it is given at a lower dose (0.01–0.05 mg/kg/min)

claims.claim: Recommendation 3.6.1 (1B): do not use recombinant human IGF-1 to prevent or treat AKI.
claims.evidence: 3.6.1: We recommend not using recombinant human (rh)IGF-1 to prevent or treat AKI. (1B)

claims.claim: Three double-blind placebo-controlled RCTs of rhIGF-1 in adults with imminent or established AKI were negative or equivocal.
claims.evidence: Based on an analysis of the three RCTs with rhIGF-1 that are currently available and which were overall negative or at least equivocal, and considering that there is no benefit and the concern over potential harm and cost associated with this drug, the Work Group recommends against its use in patients with AKI.

claims.claim: In a pilot trial, 300 U/kg i.v. erythropoietin before elective CABG reduced postoperative AKI (defined as 50% SCr increase over baseline within 5 postoperative days) from 29% to 8%.
claims.evidence: Patients received either 300 U/kg of erythropoietin or saline i.v. before surgery. AKI was defined as a 50% increase in SCr levels over baseline within the first five postoperative days. Of 71 patients, 13 developed postoperative AKI: three of the 36 patients in the erythro- poietin group (8%) and 10 of the 35 patients in the placebo group (29%; P ¼ 0.035).

claims.claim: Endre et al. randomized ICU patients to erythropoietin or placebo triggered by a urinary GGT x alkaline phosphatase biomarker product above 46.3; the primary outcome (relative average SCr increase from baseline over 4-7 days) did not differ.
claims.evidence: Randomization to either placebo or two doses of erythropoietin was triggered by an increase in the biomarker concentration product to levels above 46.3. The primary outcome was the relative average SCr increase from baseline over 4–7 days.

claims.claim: Recommendation 3.7.1 (2B): a single dose of theophylline may be given in neonates with severe perinatal asphyxia who are at high risk of AKI.
claims.evidence: 3.7.1: We suggest that a single dose of theophylline may be given in neonates with severe perinatal asphyxia, who are at high risk of AKI. (2B)

claims.claim: AKI occurs in 60% of neonates suffering from perinatal asphyxia.
claims.evidence: AKI occurs in 60% of neonates suffering from perinatal asphyxia.257

claims.claim: In three RCTs (171 term neonates), theophylline was given in the first hour of life as a single i.v. bolus of 5 mg/kg or 8 mg/kg and reduced severe renal dysfunction (17-25% vs 55-60% placebo, RR 0.3-0.41).
claims.evidence: Theophylline was uniformly administered in the first hour of life as a single i.v. bolus at a dose of 5 mg/kg259,261 or 8 mg/kg.260 ... In each study, theophylline treatment was associated with a significantly reduced risk of severe renal dysfunction (17–25% vs. 55–60% in placebo group, RR 0.3–0.41).

claims.claim: Theophylline in postasphyctic neonates did not affect patient survival and placebo controls recovered renal function completely long-term.
claims.evidence: the overall benefit from this intervention in neonatal intensive care is less evident in view of the complete long-term recovery of renal function in the placebo-treated controls and the absence of an effect on patient survival

claims.claim: In the PROTECT trial rolofylline did not benefit survival, heart-failure status, or renal function; persistent renal impairment occurred in 15.0% vs 13.7% (P=0.44).
claims.evidence: Persistent renal impairment developed in 15.0% of patients in the rolofylline group and in 13.7% of patients in the placebo group (P ¼ 0.44).

claims.claim: Seizures, a known adverse effect of A1-receptor antagonists, occurred only in the rolofylline group.
claims.evidence: Adverse-event rates were similar overall; however, only patients in the rolofylline group had seizures, a known potential adverse effect of A1-receptor antagonists.

claims.claim: Recommendation 3.8.1 (2A): do not use aminoglycosides for treatment of infections unless no suitable, less nephrotoxic alternative is available.
claims.evidence: 3.8.1: We suggest not using aminoglycosides for the treat- ment of infections unless no suitable, less nephro- toxic, therapeutic alternatives are available. (2A)

claims.claim: The risk of AKI attributable to aminoglycosides is up to 25% in some series.
claims.evidence: The risk of AKI attributable to aminoglycosides is sufficiently high (up to 25% in some series, depending upon the definition of AKI used and the population studied)271–276,278

claims.claim: Recommendation 3.8.2 (2B): in patients with normal kidney function in steady state, administer aminoglycosides as a single daily dose rather than multiple daily doses.
claims.evidence: 3.8.2: We suggest that, in patients with normal kidney function in steady state, aminoglycosides are administered as a single dose daily rather than multiple-dose daily treatment regimens. (2B)

claims.claim: Once-daily aminoglycoside dosing regimens should be administered over 60 minutes to avoid neuromuscular blockade; bolus infusions should be avoided.
claims.evidence: The high-dose, once-daily amino- glycoside regimens should be administered over 60 minutes to avoid untoward events such as neuromuscular blockade.

claims.claim: Recommendation 3.8.3 (1A): monitor aminoglycoside drug levels when multiple daily dosing is used for more than 24 hours.
claims.evidence: 3.8.3: We recommend monitoring aminoglycoside drug levels when treatment with multiple daily dosing is used for more than 24 hours. (1A)

claims.claim: Recommendation 3.8.4 (2C): monitor aminoglycoside drug levels when single-daily dosing is used for more than 48 hours.
claims.evidence: 3.8.4: We suggest monitoring aminoglycoside drug levels when treatment with single-daily dosing is used for more than 48 hours. (2C)

claims.claim: Once-daily aminoglycoside dosing is 5 mg/kg/d gentamicin and tobramycin, 6 mg/kg/d netilmicin, and 15 mg/kg/d amikacin with normal renal function.
claims.evidence: The usual dosing strategy for once-daily aminoglycosides is 5 mg/kg/d for gentamicin and tobramycin (with normal renal function); 6 mg/kg/d for netilmicin; and 15 mg/kg/d for amikacin.

claims.claim: Multiple-dose daily gentamicin/tobramycin is 1.7 mg/kg every 8 hours, with target peak 8±2 mg/ml and trough 1-2 mg/ml; amikacin peak 20±5 mg/ml and trough 5-8 mg/ml.
claims.evidence: The multiple-dose daily regimen for gentamicin and tobramycin is usually 1.7 mg/kg every 8 hours with peak blood levels at 8 ± 2 mg/ml (17±4 mmol/l) and trough of 1–2 mg/ml (2–4 mmol/l). Amikacin levels with the multiple-dose daily dosing strategy should be a peak of 20±5 mg/ml (34±9 mmol/l) and a trough of 5–8 mg/ml (9–14 mmol/l).

claims.claim: With multiple-daily dosing, Cmax should be obtained 30 minutes after a 30-minute infusion and Cmin right before the next dose.
claims.evidence: Measuring aminoglycoside levels with multiple-daily dosing strategies have been standardized for Cmax to be obtained 30 minutes after a 30-minute infusion, and Cmin right before the next dose for trough levels.

claims.claim: Recommendation 3.8.5 (2B): use topical or local applications of aminoglycosides rather than i.v. when feasible and suitable.
claims.evidence: 3.8.5: We suggest using topical or local applications of aminoglycosides (e.g., respiratory aerosols, instilled antibiotic beads), rather than i.v. application, when feasible and suitable. (2B)

claims.claim: Significant nephrotoxicity with inhaled tobramycin has been described in at least two cases.
claims.evidence: However, significant nephrotoxicity with the use of inhaled tobramycin has been described in at least two cases.326,327

claims.claim: Recommendation 3.8.6 (2A): use lipid formulations of amphotericin B rather than conventional formulations.
claims.evidence: 3.8.6: We suggest using lipid formulations of ampho- tericin B rather than conventional formulations of amphotericin B. (2A)

claims.claim: Meta-analyses concluded lipid formulations of amphotericin B are less nephrotoxic than amphotericin B deoxycholate.
claims.evidence: A detailed analysis of these various trials, and a number of meta-analyses that have analyzed this clinical question, concluded that the lipid formulations are less nephrotoxic than amphotericin B deoxycholate.344,346

claims.claim: Potassium repletion and volume repletion diminish the risk of aminoglycoside- and amphotericin B-related AKI, though clinical evidence is limited.
claims.evidence: Additionally, potassium repletion has been shown experi- mentally and clinically to diminish the risk of AKI related to aminoglycoside administration.

claims.claim: Single-dose daily aminoglycoside regimens are difficult to apply in pre-existing kidney disease and critically ill ICU patients, where frequent therapeutic drug monitoring is indicated.
claims.evidence: Single-dose daily regimens are difficult to apply in patients with pre-existing kidney disease, and patients with vacillating eGFR and hemodynamics, such as critically ill patients in the ICU setting. ... the avoidance of single-daily dosing and application of frequent therapeutic drug monitoring is indicated.322
