claims.claim: Multiple-daily dosing remains standard of care for enterococcal endocarditis, with no randomized trials comparing regimens.
claims.evidence: It should be noted that multiple-daily dosing strategies continue to be the standard of care for enterococcal endocarditis; no detailed, randomized trials have been reported comparing single-daily vs. multiple-daily regimens for enterococcal endocarditis.272,315–317

claims.claim: Amphotericin B nephrotoxicity results from afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction plus direct membrane insertion, producing enzymuria, loss of concentrating ability, renal tubular acidosis, and potassium and magnesium wasting.
claims.evidence: Amphoter- icin causes vasoconstriction of the afferent renal arteriole along with a systemic inflammatory response that may reduce renal blood flow. Amphotericin B also directly inserts into human cellular membranes, where it disrupts membrane permeability and physiology.331,332

claims.claim: KDIGO recommends azole antifungals and/or echinocandins over conventional amphotericin B for systemic mycoses or parasitic infections when efficacy is equal (1A).
claims.evidence: 3.8.7: In the treatment of systemic mycoses or parasitic infections, we recommend using azole antifungal agents and/or the echinocandins rather than conventional amphotericin B, if equal therapeutic efficacy can be assumed. (1A)

claims.claim: There is insufficient evidence on whether echinocandins, azoles, or lipid amphotericin B formulations differ in nephrotoxicity risk.
claims.evidence: There is currently insufficient evidence as to whether the echinocandins, the azoles, or the lipid formulations of amphotericin B differ significantly from each other with respect to the risk of nephrotoxicity.

claims.claim: KDIGO suggests off-pump CABG should not be selected solely to reduce perioperative AKI or need for RRT (2C).
claims.evidence: 3.9.1: We suggest that off-pump coronary artery bypass graft surgery not be selected solely for the purpose of reducing perioperative AKI or need for RRT. (2C)

claims.claim: In a 2203-patient RCT, off-pump CABG had lower graft patency than on-pump (82.6% vs 87.8%, P<0.01).
claims.evidence: the overall rate of graft patency was lower in the off-pump group than in the on-pump group (82.6% vs. 87.8%, Po0.01)

claims.claim: A meta-analysis found off-pump CABG associated with 40% lower odds of postoperative AKI and nonsignificant 33% lower odds of dialysis, with no mortality benefit.
claims.evidence: Off-pump coronary artery bypass graft was associated with a statistically significant 40% lower odds of postoperative AKI and a nonsignificant 33% lower odds for dialysis requirement.

claims.claim: KDIGO suggests not using NAC to prevent AKI in critically ill patients with hypotension (2D).
claims.evidence: 3.9.2: We suggest not using NAC to prevent AKI in critically ill patients with hypotension. (2D)

claims.claim: KDIGO recommends not using oral or i.v. NAC for prevention of postsurgical AKI (1A).
claims.evidence: 3.9.3: We recommend not using oral or i.v. NAC for prevention of postsurgical AKI. (1A)

claims.claim: NAC at doses recommended for AKI prophylaxis has no independent effect on serum creatinine or cystatin C levels.
claims.evidence: It is thus safe to conclude that NAC, in doses currently recommended for prophylaxis of AKI, has—by itself—no effect on SCr or cystatin C levels.

claims.claim: In a single RCT of 142 hypotensive ICU patients, AKI incidence was 15.5% with NAC vs 16.9% with placebo (not significant), with mortality of 10% in both arms.
claims.evidence: Patients who received NAC had an incidence of AKI of 15.5%, compared to 16.9% in those receiving placebo (NS).

claims.claim: KDIGO proposes the term contrast-induced AKI (CI-AKI) for AKI secondary to intravascular radiocontrast media exposure.
claims.evidence: proposes that the term contrast-induced acute kidney injury (CI-AKI) be used for patients developing AKI secondary to intravascular radiocontrast media exposure.

claims.claim: CI-AKI should be defined and staged using the same criteria as other AKI (Recommendations 2.1.1–2.1.2).
claims.evidence: 4.1: Define and stage AKI after administration of intra- vascular contrast media as per Recommendations 2.1.1–2.1.2. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: Patients with kidney function changes after intravascular contrast should be evaluated for CI-AKI and other possible causes of AKI.
claims.evidence: 4.1.1: In individuals who develop changes in kidney function after administration of intra- vascular contrast media, evaluate for CI-AKI as well as for other possible causes of AKI. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: The legacy contrast-induced nephropathy definition is SCr rise >=0.5 mg/dl (>=44 umol/l) or 25% increase from baseline at 48 hours after the radiological procedure.
claims.evidence: usually defined as a rise in SCr of X0.5 mg/dl (X44 mmol/l) or a 25% increase from base- line value, assessed at 48 hours after a radiological procedure.

claims.claim: In a minority of cases the peak SCr increase may occur up to 5 days after contrast exposure.
claims.evidence: It should be recognized that, in a minority of cases, the peak increase of SCr may occur up until 5 days after contrast exposure.

claims.claim: A 5% increase in SCr at 12 hours post-contrast predicted CI-AKI with 75% sensitivity, 72% specificity, AUC 0.80, OR 7.37 (95% CI 3.34-16.23).
claims.evidence: A 5% increase of its value yielded 75% sensitivity and 72% specificity, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.80 and an OR of 7.37 (95% CI 3.34–16.23) for early detection.

claims.claim: Background day-to-day SCr variation means 6-35% of inpatients not exposed to contrast would be labeled as having CI-AKI depending on threshold.
claims.evidence: Depending on the threshold criterion for CI-AKI chosen, this variation can lead to rates of 6–35% of inpatients, not exposed to contrast media, who would be labeled as having CI-AKI had they received contrast media.

claims.claim: A retrospective study found AKI incidence similar in enhanced CT (low-osmolar or iso-osmolar) and non-contrast CT groups up to a baseline SCr of 1.8 mg/dl.
claims.evidence: The incidence of AKI (defined as an increase of SCr of 0.5 mg/dl [44 mmol/l] or a X25% decrease in eGFR within 3 days after CT) was similar in all three groups (two receiving contrast agents and one not) up to a baseline SCr level of 1.8 mg/dl (159 mmol/l).

claims.claim: A cystatin C increase >=10% at 24 hours after contrast was the best early cut-off for CI-AKI risk, with NPV 100% and PPV 39%.
claims.evidence: a cut-off cystatin C increase concentration of X10% at 24 hours after contrast-media exposure was detected in 87 patients (21.2%), and was the best cut-off value for the early identification of patients at risk for CI-AKI with a negative predictive value of 100% and a positive predictive value of 39%.

claims.claim: In the Oxilan Registry, CI-AKI rates varied by definition: 3.3%, 10.2%, 7.6%, and 10.5% (composite).
claims.evidence: CI-AKI rates were 3.3% (SCr increase 40.5 mg/dl [444 mmol/l]), 10.2% (SCr increase 425%), 7.6% (eGFR decrease 425%), and 10.5% (composite), respectively.

claims.claim: In patients with normal renal function, even with diabetes, CI-AKI risk is low (1-2%); risk may reach 25% with pre-existing renal impairment or other risk factors.
claims.evidence: It is accepted that, in patients with normal renal function— even in the presence of diabetes—the risk for CI-AKI is low (1–2%).392 However, the incidence may be as high as 25% in patients with pre-existing renal impairment

claims.claim: CI-AKI was the third most common cause of new AKI in hospitalized patients, responsible for 11% of cases.
claims.evidence: CI-AKI was described as the third most common cause of new AKI in hospitalized patients (after decreased renal perfusion and nephrotoxic medications) and was responsible for 11% of cases.

claims.claim: In 75 ICU patients with normal baseline SCr exposed to i.v. low-osmolar contrast CT, SCr increased >25% in 18%, with no change in the non-contrast control group.
claims.evidence: In a group of 75 ICU patients with a normal baseline SCr who were exposed to CT scans with an i.v. low-osmolar contrast medium, an increase in SCr 425% was recorded in 18% of the patients.

claims.claim: Hospital mortality was 7.1% in CI-AKI and 35.7% in those requiring dialysis; 2-year mortality in dialysis-requiring patients was 81.2%.
claims.evidence: the hospital mortality was 7.1% in CI-AKI and 35.7% in patients who required dialysis. By 2 years, the mortality rate in patients who required dialysis was 81.2%.

claims.claim: KDIGO recommends assessing CI-AKI risk and screening for pre-existing kidney function impairment in all patients considered for intravascular iodinated contrast administration.
claims.evidence: 4.2.1: Assess the risk for CI-AKI and, in particular, screen for pre-existing impairment of kidney function in all patients who are considered for a procedure that requires intravascular (i.v. or i.a.) administration of iodinated contrast medium. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: The CI-AKI Consensus Working Panel recommended precautions for baseline eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2; the Work Group notes this threshold could probably be lowered to 45 ml/min/1.73 m2.
claims.evidence: The CI-AKI Consensus Working Panel410 recommended that precautions to reduce the risk should be implemented in patients with a baseline eGFRo60 ml/min per 1.73 m2. In light of more recent information, this threshold could probably be lowered to 45 ml/min per 1.73 m2.

claims.claim: Of 310 patients with negative urine protein and no relevant history, none had SCr >2.0 mg/dl and only 1% had SCr >1.7 mg/dl.
claims.evidence: Of 310 patients with a negative urine protein test and no history of diseases poten- tially associated with renal impairment, none had a SCr level 42.0 mg/dl (4177 mmol/l), and only 1% had a level 41.7 mg/dl (4150 mmol/l).

claims.claim: There is insufficient evidence to recommend discontinuing ACE-I or ARB prior to contrast-media administration.
claims.evidence: There are conflicting data on the impact of ACE-I or ARB but, overall, there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend discontinuation of these medications prior to contrast-media administration.

claims.claim: Repeated contrast exposure should be delayed 48 hours without risk factors and 72 hours with diabetes or pre-existing chronic renal dysfunction.
claims.evidence: Repeated exposure should be delayed for 48 hours in patients without risk factors for CI-AKI, and for 72 hours in those with diabetes mellitus or pre-existing chronic renal dysfunc- tion.

claims.claim: Contrast media administration should be delayed in patients with circulatory collapse or CHF until hemodynamic status is corrected.
claims.evidence: When possible, the administration of contrast media should be delayed in patients with circulatory collapse or CHF until their hemodynamic status is corrected.

claims.claim: KDIGO does not express a preference for isotonic saline versus isotonic bicarbonate for CI-AKI prevention; either can be used.
claims.evidence: the Work Group not to express a preference for or against one solution (isotonic saline or isotonic bicarbonate). Thus, either can be used for the prevention of CI-AKI.

claims.claim: KDIGO suggests oral NAC together with i.v. isotonic crystalloids in patients at increased risk of CI-AKI (2D).
claims.evidence: 4.4.3: We suggest using oral NAC, together with i.v. iso- tonic crystalloids, in patients at increased risk of CI-AKI. (2D)

claims.claim: KDIGO suggests not using theophylline to prevent CI-AKI (2C).
claims.evidence: 4.4.4: We suggest not using theophylline to prevent CI-AKI. (2C)

claims.claim: KDIGO recommends not using fenoldopam to prevent CI-AKI (1B).
claims.evidence: 4.4.5: We recommend not using fenoldopam to prevent CI-AKI. (1B)

claims.claim: KDIGO suggests not using prophylactic IHD or hemofiltration for contrast-media removal in patients at increased risk of CI-AKI (2C).
claims.evidence: 4.5.1: We suggest not using prophylactic intermittent hemodialysis (IHD) or hemofiltration (HF) for contrast-media removal in patients at increased risk for CI-AKI. (2C)

claims.claim: There is no current evidence that oral or i.v. NAC alters mortality or need for RRT after contrast-media administration.
claims.evidence: At present, there is no current evidence that either oral or i.v. NAC can alter mortality or need for RRT after contrast-media administration to patients at risk for CI-AKI.

claims.claim: High-dose NAC is defined in meta-analysis as a daily dose greater than 1200 mg or a single periprocedural dose greater than 600 mg within 4 hours of contrast exposure.
claims.evidence: A meta-analysis497 of studies using high doses of NAC defined the latter as a daily dose greater than 1200 mg or a single periprocedural dose greater than 600 mg (periprocedural being described as immediately or within 4 hours of the planned contrast exposure).

claims.claim: No FDA label exists for NAC as a preventive drug for AKI.
claims.evidence: It should also be remembered that no FDA label is available for NAC as a preventive drug of AKI.

claims.claim: In Briguori et al., CI-AKI occurred in 9.9% with saline+NAC, 1.9% with bicarbonate+NAC (P=0.019), and 10.3% with saline+ascorbic acid+NAC.
claims.evidence: CI-AKI occurred in 9.9% of the saline plus NAC group, in 1.9% of the bicarbonate/NAC group (P ¼ 0.019 vs. saline plus NAC group), and in 10.3% of the saline plus ascorbic acid plus NAC group

claims.claim: In Maioli et al. (n=502, CrCl <60 mL/min), CI-AKI occurred in 10% with sodium bicarbonate and 11.5% with saline, suggesting bicarbonate is not more efficient than saline.
claims.evidence: CI- AKI occurred in 10.8%; 10% were treated with sodium bicarbonate and 11.5% with saline... Based on this last prospective study, bicarbonate does not seem to be more efficient than saline.

claims.claim: Isotonic bicarbonate solutions are made by adding 154 ml of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate to 846 ml of 5% glucose, giving 154 mmol/l sodium and bicarbonate.
claims.evidence:
isotonic bicarbonate solutions are usually composed by adding 154 ml of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate (i.e., 1 
mmol/ ml) to 846 ml of 5% glucose solution, resulting in a final sodium and bicarbonate concentration of 154 mmol/l each.

claims.claim: Combination NAC plus i.v. sodium bicarbonate reduced CI-AKI by 35% (RR 0.65; 95% CI 0.40-1.05) but did not reduce dialysis-requiring renal failure (RR 0.47; 95% CI 0.16-1.41).
claims.evidence: combination treatment of NAC with i.v. sodium bicarbonate reduced CI-AKI by 35% compared to the other above-mentioned combinations (RR 0.65; 95% CI 0.40–1.05). However, the combination of NAC plus sodium bicarbonate did not significantly reduce renal failure requiring dialysis (RR 0.47; 95% CI 0.16–1.41).

claims.claim: Meta-analyses of theophylline showed only a nonsignificant trend toward renoprotection (Bagshaw OR 0.4, CI 0.14-1.16; Kelly OR 0.49, CI 0.23-1.06).
claims.evidence: The incidence of CI-AKI tended to be lower (Bagshaw: OR 0.4, CI 0.14–1.16, P ¼ 0.09; Kelly: OR 0.49, CI 0.23–1.06, P ¼ 0.14)

claims.claim: In a double-blind trial of 315 patients, fenoldopam showed no difference in CI-AKI within 96 hours (33.6% vs placebo 30.1%) or dialysis, rehospitalization, or 30-day death.
claims.evidence:
There was no significant difference in the incidence of CI-AKI within 96 hours in the two groups (fenoldopam, 
33.6%; placebo, 30.1%) or in the rates of dialysis, rehospitalization, or death at 30 days.

claims.claim: Reinecke et al. found CI-AKI in 6.1% fluids only, 15.9% with IHD, and 5.3% with NAC, concluding prophylactic IHD provided no benefit and probable harm.
claims.evidence: was 6.1% in the fluids-only group, 15.9% with IHD treatment, and 5.3% in the NAC group (intention- to-treat analysis; P ¼ 0.008)

claims.claim: A single hemodialysis session removes 60-90% of contrast media.
claims.evidence:
Contrast 
media can be efficiently removed from blood by IHD and a single session effectively removes 60–90% of contrast media.516,517

claims.claim: Removal of creatinine during HF or IHD confounds the observed lower incidence of CI-AKI.
claims.evidence: The effective removal of creatinine during HF or IHD makes it difficult to be certain that an observed lower incidence of CI-AKI is not related to the transport removal of creatinine during the procedure.

claims.claim: KDIGO advises initiating RRT emergently when life-threatening changes in fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance exist (Not Graded).
claims.evidence: 5.1.1: Initiate RRT emergently when life-threatening changes in fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance exist. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: KDIGO advises considering clinical context and laboratory trends rather than single BUN and creatinine thresholds when deciding to start RRT (Not Graded).
claims.evidence: 5.1.2: Consider the broader clinical context, the presence of conditions that can be modified with RRT, and trends of laboratory tests—rather than single BUN and creatinine thresholds alone—when making the decision to start RRT. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: Metabolic acidosis associated with AKI can usually be corrected with bicarbonate and rarely requires urgent dialysis unless accompanied by volume overload or uremia.
claims.evidence: metabolic acidosis associated with AKI can usually be corrected with bicarbonate and should rarely require urgent dialysis if not accompanied by volume overload or uremia.527

claims.claim: No standard pH or bicarbonate criteria exist for initiating dialysis for metabolic acidosis.
claims.evidence: As the pH and bicarbonate values to initiate dialysis for metabolic acidosis are not supported by evidence, no standard criteria for initiating dialysis for acidosis exist.

claims.claim: In Bouman et al., early RRT initiation was defined as starting within 12 hours of oliguria (<30 ml/h for 6 hours).
claims.evidence: The early initiation group started RRT within 12 hours of oliguria (o30 ml/h for 6 hours, not respond- ing to

claims.claim: A forced euvolemic diuresis protocol with mannitol and furosemide significantly increased CI-AKI risk, and furosemide should preferably be stopped before angiography.
claims.evidence: A recent study using a so-called forced euvolemic diuresis protocol including mannitol and furosemide led to a signi- ficantly increased risk of CI-AKI.415 It can be advised that such strategy should be abandoned, and that furose- mide therapy should preferably be stopped before angio- graphy.

claims.claim: The Mehran risk score assigns integer points: hypotension 5, IABP 5, CHF 5, age >75 years 4, anemia 3, diabetes 3, contrast volume 1 per 100 ml, SCr >1.5 mg/dl 4, or eGFR <60 (2/4/6 by band).
claims.evidence: Hypotension 5 IABP 5 CHF 5 Age 475 years 4 Anemia 3 Diabetes 3 Contrast-media volume 1 per 100 ml SCr 41.5 mg/dl (4132.6 mmol/l) 4 or eGFR o60 ml/min per 1.73 m2 2 for 40–60 4 for 20–39 6 for o20

claims.claim: Mehran score low risk is cumulative score <5 and high risk is >=16.
claims.evidence: Note: Low risk: cumulative score o5; high risk: cumulative score 416.

claims.claim: CI-AKI occurrence in the Mehran development set was 13.1%, ranging 7.5% to 57.3% between low and high risk scores.
claims.evidence: The overall occurrence of CI-AKI in the development set of the score was 13.1% (range 7.5% to 57.3% for a low [p5] and high [X16] risk score, respectively); the rate of CI-AKI increased exponentially with increasing risk score.

claims.claim: Risk of CI-AKI rises exponentially with the number of risk factors present.
claims.evidence: Most risk factors for CI-AKI can be detected by history-taking and physical examination, and the risk rises exponentially with the number of risk factors present.416

claims.claim: KDIGO recommendation 4.2.2 (Not Graded): consider alternative imaging methods in patients at increased risk for CI-AKI.
claims.evidence: 4.2.2: Consider alternative imaging methods in patients at increased risk for CI-AKI. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: EMA contraindicated gadodiamide at GFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m2 and warned for GFR 30–60.
claims.evidence: the European Medicines Agency stated a contraindication for use of gadodiamide in patients with a GFR o30 ml/min per 1.73 m2, and issued a warning for its use in patients who have a GFR between 30 and 60 ml/min per 1.73 m2

claims.claim: FDA labeling describes NSF risk after Gd exposure at GFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m2 and in AKI of any severity due to hepatorenal syndrome or perioperative liver transplantation.
claims.evidence: New labeling describes the risk for NSF following expo- sure to Gd in patients with a GFR o30 ml/min per 1.73 m2 and in patients with AKI of any severity due to hepato-renal syndrome or in the perioperative liver trans- plantation period.

claims.claim: Macrocyclic gadolinium chelate (gadoteridol) is preferred over linear chelates; gadodiamide carries the highest NSF risk.
claims.evidence: Use of a macrocyclic chelate (gadoteridol in the USA), is preferred over linear chelates. The risk associated with the various Gd-containing agents is likely different. Gadodiamide, the linear nonionic chelate–- based formulation, maintains the highest risk

claims.claim: IHD after gadolinium exposure removes >95% of plasma Gd but no data support NSF prevention; PD clears these agents poorly.
claims.evidence: This recommendation is based on the pharmaco- kinetics of Gd and the theoretical benefit of removing it with IHD (495% plasma clearance). PD clears these agents rather poorly.

claims.claim: KDIGO recommendation 4.3.1 (Not Graded): use the lowest possible dose of contrast medium in patients at risk for CI-AKI.
claims.evidence: 4.3.1: Use the lowest possible dose of contrast medium in patients at risk for CI-AKI. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: A g-I/eGFR ratio <1 was associated with 3% CI-AKI risk versus 25% at ratio >=1.
claims.evidence: At a ratio o1, the risk of CI-AKI was 3%, while it was 25% at a ratio X1. This, and other preliminary studies, indicate that a g-I/GFR ratio o1 may be relatively safe in a patient without multiple risk factors.436–438

claims.claim: Maximum contrast-medium dose was calculated as (5 x body weight [kg]) / SCr, and CI-AKI was associated with both contrast volume and the contrast-medium ratio.
claims.evidence: the maximum contrast-medium dose was calculated according to the formula (5  body weight [kg]) C SCr, and the contrast-medium ratio—defined as the ratio between the contrast-medium volume administered and the maximum dose calculated—was assessed. Development of CI-AKI was associated with both contrast-medium volume and ratio.

claims.claim: CI-AKI risk is greater after arterial than venous contrast administration; i.v. contrast CI-AKI incidence was about 5% in moderate CKD with low-osmolar media.
claims.evidence: The risk of CI-AKI appears to be greater after arterial compared to venous administration of contrast media. ... The overall incidence of CI-AKI in these studies, using the current generation of low-osmolar contrast media, was about 5%.

claims.claim: KDIGO recommendation 4.3.2 (1B): use iso-osmolar or low-osmolar rather than high-osmolar iodinated contrast media in patients at increased risk of CI-AKI.
claims.evidence: 4.3.2: We recommend using either iso-osmolar or low- osmolar iodinated contrast media, rather than high-osmolar iodinated contrast media in patients at increased risk of CI-AKI. (1B)

claims.claim: CI-AKI was generally defined in the reviewed studies as an SCr increase >25% or 0.5 mg/dl within 72 hours of contrast administration without alternative etiology.
claims.evidence: We used the general definitions of CI-AKI provided in the studies (an increase in SCr by 425% or 0.5 mg/dl [44.2 mmol/l]) occurring within 72 hours after contrast- medium administration, in the absence of an alternative etiology for the decrease in kidney function.

claims.claim: Meta-analysis of iodixanol vs low-osmolar contrast media gave pooled RR 0.68 (95% CI 0.46-1.01; P=0.06); iodixanol was superior only versus iohexol (RR 0.38; 95% CI 0.21-0.68).
claims.evidence: The pooled RR was 0.68 (95% CI 0.46–1.01; P ¼ 0.06). ... in all three studies in which iohexol was the low-osmolar contrast medium used, the risk of CI-AKI was significantly lower with iodixanol (RR 0.38; 95% CI 0.21–0.68; Po0.01).

claims.claim: For i.v. administration there was no benefit of iodixanol vs low-osmolar contrast media (RR 1.08; 95% CI 0.62-1.89; P=0.79).
claims.evidence: showed no statistically significant difference for CI-AKI (RR 1.08; 95% CI 0.62–1.89; P ¼ 0.79)

claims.claim: KDIGO recommendation 4.4.1 (1A): i.v. volume expansion with isotonic sodium chloride or sodium bicarbonate rather than no volume expansion in patients at increased risk for CI-AKI.
claims.evidence: 4.4.1: We recommend i.v. volume expansion with either isotonic sodium chloride or sodium bicarbonate solutions, rather than no i.v. volume expansion, in patients at increased risk for CI-AKI. (1A)

claims.claim: Most studies suggest fluids should be started at least 1 h before and continued 3-6 hours after contrast-media administration.
claims.evidence: most studies suggest that the fluids should be started at least 1 h before and continued for 3–6 hours after contrast-media administration.

claims.claim: To achieve urine flow of at least 150 ml/h, >=1.0-1.5 ml/kg/h i.v. fluid is needed for 3-12 hours before and 6-12 hours after contrast exposure.
claims.evidence: in order to achieve a urine flow rate of at least 150 ml/h, X1.0–1.5 ml/kg/h of i.v. fluid has to be administered for 3–12 hours before and 6–12 hours after contrast-media exposure.

claims.claim: Isotonic 0.9% saline reduced CI-AKI compared to 0.45% saline in dextrose in 1620 patients undergoing coronary angiography.
claims.evidence: Mueller et al.469 found that i.v. 0.9% saline solution, compared to 0.45% saline solution in dextrose, in 1620 patients undergoing coronary angiography significantly reduced CI-AKI.

claims.claim: A systematic review of 23 trials (3563 patients, 396 CI-AKI events) found pooled RR 0.62 (95% CI 0.45-0.86) for bicarbonate, with significant heterogeneity and no clear effect on dialysis, heart failure, or mortality.
claims.evidence: Twenty-three published and unpublished trials with information on 3563 patients and 396 CI-AKI events were included. The pooled RR was 0.62 (95% CI 0.45–0.86), with evidence of significant heterogeneity across studies. ... No clear effects of treatment on the risk for dialysis, heart failure, and total mortality were identified.

claims.claim: Small, poor-quality studies assessing outcomes soon after contrast were more likely to suggest bicarbonate benefit.
claims.evidence: Meta-regression showed that small, poor-quality studies that assessed outcomes soon after contrast-media administration were more likely to suggest the benefit of bicarbonate (Po0.05 for all).

claims.claim: In a propensity analysis only 40.0% of patients received pre/post contrast i.v. fluids (91.2% with coronary angiography vs 16.6% with CT), and i.v. fluid use was associated with a reduced rate of CI-AKI.
claims.evidence: Pre– and post–contrast-media administra- tion i.v. fluids were given to only 264 of 660 study patients (40.0%), more commonly with coronary angiography than with CT (91.2% vs. 16.6%). ... In a propensity analysis, the use of i.v. fluids was associated with a reduced rate of CI-AKI.

claims.claim: Ozcan et al. found CI-AKI in 4.5% with sodium bicarbonate versus 13.6% with sodium chloride (P=0.036; adjusted risk ratio 0.29, P=0.043).
claims.evidence: The incidence of CI-AKI, defined as an increase in SCr level 425% or 0.5 mg/dl (44.2 mmol/l) after 48 hours was significantly lower in the sodium bicarbonate group (4.5%) compared to sodium chloride alone (13.6%, P ¼ 0.036).

claims.claim: In a randomized comparison of citrate vs heparin in 142 CVVH circuits, circuit survival did not differ but major bleeding and transfusion need were significantly greater with heparin.
claims.evidence: Neither circuit survival nor the reasons for disconnecting the CVVH circuit differed significantly between the two groups. However, the number of major bleedings and the need for transfusion was significantly greater in the heparin group.

claims.claim: In a 200-patient RCT of postdilution CVVH, safety was significantly better with citrate than nadroparin (2 vs 20 patients requiring anticoagulant change), with equal circuit survival.
claims.evidence: Safety was significantly better in the citrate group with only two patients requiring a change in anticoagulation regimen vs. 20 patients in the nadroparin group (P40.001).

claims.claim: Adverse events in the citrate arm were citrate accumulation (n=1) and early clotting (n=1); in the nadroparin arm bleeding (n=16) and severe thrombocytopenia (n=4).
claims.evidence: Adverse events were citrate accumulation (n ¼ 1) and early clotting due to protocol violation (n ¼ 1) in the citrate group, and bleeding (n ¼ 16) or severe thrombocytopenia (n ¼ 4) in the nadroparin group.

claims.claim: Regional citrate anticoagulation use remains limited to 0–20% of patients/treatments in recent surveys and large trials.
claims.evidence: In recently published surveys or large clinical trials, the use of regional citrate antic- oagulation is still limited to 0–20% of the patients/ treatments.

claims.claim: KDIGO recommends citrate for CRRT anticoagulation only in patients without shock or severe liver failure and in centers with an established citrate protocol.
claims.evidence: We, therefore, only recommend the use of citrate for anticoagulation during CRRT in patients that do not have shock or severe liver failure, and in centers that have an established protocol for citrate anticoagulation.

claims.claim: Unfractionated heparin remains the most widely used anticoagulant during CRRT, mostly as a prefilter infusion with large dose variability.
claims.evidence: Unfractionated heparin still remains the most widely used anticoagulant during CRRT,562,563,607 mostly administered as a prefilter infusion, with large variability in the administered doses.

claims.claim: The relationship among heparin dose, aPTT, filter survival and bleeding complications is not straightforward, but aPTT is commonly measured for safety and adapted to bleeding risk.
claims.evidence: the clinician should realize that the relationship among heparin dose, aPTT, filter survival, and bleeding complications is not straightfor- ward,574,614–619 but it is common practice to measure aPTT ... for safety reasons and to adapt the target to the bleeding risk of the patient.

claims.claim: In a crossover trial of predilution CVVH (37 completers), mean filter life was 21.7 h with unfractionated heparin vs 30.6 h with enoxaparin (P=0.017), with similar low bleeding and similar costs.
claims.evidence: In the 37 patients that completed both treatment arms, mean filter life was 21.7 hours with heparin and 30.6 hours with enoxaparin (P ¼ 0.017).

claims.claim: Clinical studies found no correlation between anti–Factor Xa levels and filter life, questioning anti–Factor Xa monitoring for efficacy.
claims.evidence: Interestingly, these clinical studies did not find a correlation between anti–Factor Xa levels and filter life, questioning the value of anti–Factor Xa monitoring with regard to efficacy.

claims.claim: Regional heparinization with protamine neutralization is cumbersome, risks rebound, and exposes patients to side-effects of both drugs; it is not recommended.
claims.evidence: It is cumbersome and difficult to titrate because heparin has a much longer half-life than protamine, inducing a risk of rebound. In addition, it exposes the patient to the side-effects of both heparin (mainly the risk of HIT) and protamine ... and is therefore not recommended.

claims.claim: If HIT is likely all heparins must be stopped, including heparin lock solutions for dialysis or other catheters.
claims.evidence: If HIT is likely, all heparins have to be stopped, including any ‘‘heparin lock’’ solutions for dialysis or other catheters.

claims.claim: Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor eliminated by the liver with a short half-life that can be monitored with aPTT.
claims.evidence: Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor, is eliminated by the liver, has a short half-life, and can be monitored with aPTT.

claims.claim: The pediatric citrate protocol prescribes ACD-A at blood pump rate (ml/min x min/h) x 1.5 and calcium chloride at blood pump rate x 0.6.
claims.evidence: ACD rate ðml=hÞ ¼ blood pump rate ðml= min  min =hÞ1:5 ... Calcium chloride ðml=hÞ ¼ blood pump rate ðml= min  min =hÞ0:6

claims.claim: In pediatric CRRT, heparin- and citrate-based anticoagulation protocols confer equitable filter survival, and either is clearly supported over no anticoagulation.
claims.evidence: The ppCRRT Registry Group has shown that heparin- and citrate-based anticoagulation protocols have been shown to confer equitable filter survival in pediatric CRRT, and the use of either is clearly supported over the use of no anticoagulation schemes.

claims.claim: Optimal dialysis catheter length is 12–15 cm for the right internal jugular vein, 15–20 cm for the left internal jugular vein, and 19–24 cm for the femoral vein.
claims.evidence: This means that the optimal length is 12–15 cm for the right internal jugular vein, 15–20 cm for the left internal jugular vein, and 19–24 cm for the femoral vein.

claims.claim: In a randomized trial of 750 AKI patients, catheter colonization at removal did not differ between femoral and jugular sites; bloodstream infection was 2.3 vs 1.5 per 1000 catheter-days.
claims.evidence: The incidence of catheter colonization at removal (the primary end-point) was not significantly different between the femoral and jugular group. ... Blood- stream infection did not differ between the groups (2.3 per 1000 catheter-days for jugular and 1.5 per 1000 catheter-days for femoral)

claims.claim: Colonization risk varied by BMI tertile: lowest BMI tertile had higher colonization with jugular, highest BMI tertile with femoral catheters.
claims.evidence: When stratified according to body mass index (BMI), those within the lowest BMI tertile had a higher incidence of colonization with the jugular site, whereas those within the highest BMI tertile had the highest colonization rate with femoral catheters.

claims.claim: Patients who may undergo kidney transplantation should not have a femoral catheter placed, to avoid iliac vein stenosis.
claims.evidence: Another point to consider is that any patient who has the option of undergoing a kidney transplantation should not have a femoral catheter placed to avoid stenosis of the iliac vein, to which the transplanted kidney’s vein is anato- mized.

claims.claim: Complications of central venous catheterization include arterial puncture (0.5–6%), hematoma (0.1–4.4%), hemothorax (0.4–0.6%), pneumothorax (0.1–3.1%), with 10–20% of insertion attempts unsuccessful.
claims.evidence: Compli- cations of central venous catheterization include arterial puncture (0.5–6%), hematoma (0.1–4.4%), hemothorax (0.4–0.6%), pneumothorax (0.1–3.1%), and up to 10–20% of insertion attempts are not successful.

claims.claim: The correct tip position of a semirigid dialysis catheter is at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium.
claims.evidence: The correct position of the tip of a semirigid dialysis catheter is at the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrium, allowing the catheter to run in parallel with the long axis of the superior vena cava.

claims.claim: CDC, NHS and IDSA guidelines strongly recommend against topical antibiotic ointment for CVC care because of potential to promote fungal infections and antimicrobial resistance.
claims.evidence: the CDC, National Health Service, and Infectious Diseases Society of America guidelines strongly recommend against topical antibiotic ointment for the care of CVC, because of their potential to promote fungal infections and antimicro- bial resistance.

claims.claim: In two recent large randomized trials the mean duration of RRT for AKI was 12–13 days, which likely does not justify initial tunneled catheters in all patients.
claims.evidence: In two recent large randomized trials, the mean duration of RRT for AKI was 12–13 days.562,563 This probably does not justify the burden of an initial tunneled catheter in all patients with AKI receiving RRT.

claims.claim: Pediatric CRRT circuit survival is favored by larger catheter size; two single-lumen 5 F catheters gave extremely poor circuit survival and should be avoided.
claims.evidence: the Prospective Pediatric CRRT Registry group showed extremely poor circuit survival with two single- lumen 5 F catheters; these catheters should therefore be avoided.

claims.claim: Biocompatible membranes (modified cellulosic or synthetic polyacrylonitrile, polysulfone, PMMA) produce less complement and cytokine activation and decrease oxidative stress.
claims.evidence: These ‘‘biocompatible membranes’’ (or less bioincompatible membranes) produce less complement and cytokine activation, and decrease oxidative stress.

claims.claim: A randomized trial of early vs late RRT initiation found no differences in ICU or hospital mortality or renal recovery, but was underpowered.
claims.evidence: The study did not find differences in ICU or hospital mortality, or in renal recovery among survivors, but was clearly too small to allow for definitive conclusions (Suppl Table 30).

claims.claim: In the PICARD cohort, RRT initiation at higher BUN was associated with increased risk of death (RR 1.85).
claims.evidence: initiation of RRT at higher BUN (476 mg/dl [blood urea427.1 mmol/l]) was associated with an increased risk of death (RR 1.85; 95% CI 1.16–2.96).539

claims.claim: In the BEST KIDNEY multicenter study, timing of RRT by serum urea showed no mortality difference, but late initiation relative to ICU admission was associated with higher adjusted mortality (OR 1.95).
claims.evidence: Timing by serum urea showed no significant difference in mortality. However, when timing was analyzed in relation to ICU admission, late RRT was associated with greater crude mortality (72.8% late vs. 62.3% delayed vs. 59% early, P ¼ 0.001) and covariate-adjusted mortality (OR 1.95; 95% CI 1.30–2.92; P ¼ 0.001).

claims.claim: Traditional CKD-derived indications for RRT are not necessarily valid in AKI; volume overload may indicate RRT without BUN or SCr elevation.
claims.evidence: Traditional indications for RRT, developed for patients with advanced CKD, are not necessarily valid in the context of AKI. For instance, massive volume overload resulting from volume resuscitation may be an indication for RRT even in the absence of significant elevations in BUN or SCr.

claims.claim: KDIGO lists four goals of treating AKI with RRT: homeostasis, preventing further kidney insults, permitting renal recovery, and allowing other supportive measures.
claims.evidence: The treatment of AKI with RRT has the following goals: i) to maintain fluid and electrolyte, acid-base, and solute homeo- stasis; ii) to prevent further insults to the kidney; iii) to permit renal recovery; and iv) to allow other supportive measures (e.g., antibiotics, nutrition support) to proceed without limitation or complication.

claims.claim: In PICARD, survivors had lower fluid accumulation at dialysis initiation than nonsurvivors (8.8% vs 14.2% of baseline body weight), with adjusted OR for death 2.07.
claims.evidence: Survivors had lower fluid accumulation at dialysis initiation compared to nonsurvivors (8.8% vs. 14.2% of baseline body weight; P ¼ 0.01 adjusted for dialysis modality and severity score). The adjusted OR for death associated with fluid overload at dialysis initiation was 2.07 (95% CI 1.27–3.37).83

claims.claim: Plasma NGAL had an AUC-ROC of 0.82 for prediction of RRT requirement.
claims.evidence: Plasma neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin was shown to have an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.82 for the prediction of RRT requirement.551

claims.claim: In children on RRT, mortality rose with fluid overload category: 29.6% (<10%), 43.1% (10-20%), 65.6% (>20%).
claims.evidence: increased mortality with increasing fluid overload in 297 children treated with RRT: 29.6% mortality with less than 10% fluid overload, 43.1% with 10–20% fluid overload, and 65.6% with 420% fluid overload.548

claims.claim: In a multicenter pediatric study, percentage fluid accumulation at CRRT initiation was lower in survivors (14.2% vs 25.4%) after adjustment for illness severity.
claims.evidence: the percentage fluid accumulation at CRRT initiation is significantly lower in survivors vs. non-survivors (14.2 ± 15.9% vs. 25.4 ± 32.9%; Po0.03) even after adjustment for severity of illness.

claims.claim: KDIGO recommendation 5.2.1 (Not Graded): discontinue RRT when kidney function has recovered adequately or RRT is no longer consistent with goals of care.
claims.evidence: 5.2.1: Discontinue RRT when it is no longer required, either because intrinsic kidney function has recov- ered to the point that it is adequate to meet patient needs, or because RRT is no longer consistent with the goals of care. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: Mean duration of RRT in two recent large RCTs was 12-13 days.
claims.evidence: The mean duration of RRT in two recent large RCTs was 12–13 days.562,563

claims.claim: During CRRT, continuous solute clearance of 25-35 ml/min stabilizes serum markers after 48 hours, allowing reliable native CrCl measurement.
claims.evidence: In CRRT, continuous solute clearance of 25–35 ml/min will stabilize serum markers after 48 hours. This allows more reliable measurements of CrCl by the native kidneys during CRRT.

claims.claim: A measured 24-hour CrCl greater than 15 ml/min was associated with successful CRRT termination, defined as no CRRT need for at least 14 days.
claims.evidence: a CrCl (measured over 24 hours) 415 ml/min was associated with successful termination of CRRT, defined as the absence of CRRT requirement for at least 14 days following cessation.567

claims.claim: Urine output was the most significant predictor of successful RRT termination (OR 1.078 per 100 ml/d), with predictive ability reduced by diuretic use.
claims.evidence: Multivariate logistic regression identified urine output as the most significant predictor of successful termination (OR 1.078 per 100 ml/d). Not surprisingly, the predictive ability of urine output was negatively affected by the use of diuretics.196

claims.claim: KDIGO recommendation 5.2.2 (2B): suggest not using diuretics to enhance kidney function recovery or reduce duration/frequency of RRT.
claims.evidence: 5.2.2: We suggest not using diuretics to enhance kidney function recovery, or to reduce the duration or frequency of RRT. (2B)

claims.claim: In the only RCT of diuretics during RRT, furosemide 0.5 mg/kg/h increased urine volume and sodium excretion but did not change need for repeated CVVH or renal recovery.
claims.evidence: Patients treated with furosemide (n ¼ 36) had a significantly increased urinary volume and greater sodium excretion compared to placebo-treated patients (n ¼ 35). However, there were no differences in need for repeated CVVH, or renal recovery during ICU or hospital stay.195

claims.claim: KDIGO recommendation 5.3.1.1 (1B): use anticoagulation during RRT in AKI if no increased bleeding risk, no impaired coagulation, and not already systemically anticoagulated.
claims.evidence: 5.3.1.1: We recommend using anticoagulation during RRT in AKI if a patient does not have an increased bleeding risk or impaired coagulation and is not already receiving systemic anticoagulation. (1B)

claims.claim: In two recent large trials, 50-60% of AKI patients requiring RRT were treated without anticoagulant.
claims.evidence: In two recent large trials 50–60% of AKI patients requiring RRT were treated without anticoagulant.562,563

claims.claim: No specific cut-off points exist for platelet count, aPTT, INR, or fibrinogen to indicate RRT without anticoagulation.
claims.evidence: However, no specific cut-off points have been determined for platelet count, aPTT, International Normalized Ratio, fibrino- gen, or other coagulation factors that would indicate the possibility to perform RRT without anticoagulation.

claims.claim: A meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found unfractionated and low-molecular-weight heparin equally safe for bleeding (RR 0.96) and equally effective at preventing extracorporeal thrombosis (RR 1.15) in chronic IHD.
claims.evidence: A recent meta-analysis of 11 RCTs comparing unfractio- nated to low-molecular-weight heparin in chronic IHD concluded that both are equally safe in terms of bleed- ing complications (RR 0.96; CI 0.27–3.43) and as effective in preventing extracorporeal thrombosis (RR 1.15; CI 0.7–1.91).586

claims.claim: In an RCT of predilution CVVHDF, citrate anticoagulation improved filter survival versus heparin (124.5 vs 38.3 hours) and fewer filters clotted (16.7% vs 53.5%).
claims.evidence: significantly improved filter survival (124.5 hours vs. 38.3 hours; Po0.001). In addition, significantly less citrate- anticoagulated filters were terminated for clotting (16.7% vs. 53.5%).

claims.claim: A mole of trisodium citrate produces the same buffering effect as 3 moles of sodium bicarbonate.
claims.evidence: a mole of trisodium citrate produces the same buffering effect as 3 moles of sodium bicarbonate; whereas preparations of citrate, including hydrogen citrate, have proportionally less buffering effect.

claims.claim: Withdrawal of life support accounted for 72% of deaths in a database of 383 AKI patients.
claims.evidence: Analysis of a database of 383 AKI patients shows withdrawal of life support in 72% of deaths.565

claims.claim: Non-anticoagulant strategies to prolong filter survival include good vascular access, saline flushes, predilution, high blood flow rates, diffusive treatment, and reduced blood-air contact.
claims.evidence: These include a good functioning vascular access, the reduction of blood viscosity and hemoconcentration by saline flushes, predilution, high blood flow rates, diffusive treatment, the reduction of blood-air contact in the bubble trap, and assuring prompt reaction to alarms.577,578

claims.claim: The KDIGO AKI guideline evidence review was conducted by an Evidence Review Team at the Tufts Center for Kidney Disease Guideline Development and Implementation, directed by Katrin Uhlig.
claims.evidence: Katrin Uhlig, MD, MS, is the Director, Guideline Develop- ment at the Tufts Center for Kidney Disease Guideline Development and Implementation, Boston, MA

claims.claim: The KDIGO Evidence Rating Group was co-chaired in 2005 to develop a consensus on grading of KDIGO guidelines.
claims.evidence: In 2005, she co-chaired the KDIGO Evidence Rating Group to develop a consensus on grading of KDIGO guidelines.

claims.claim: The draft guideline underwent external review by named individuals and organizations, and participation in review does not constitute endorsement.
claims.evidence: Participation in the review does not necessarily constitute endorsement of the content of this report by above indivi- duals or the organization or institution they represent.

claims.claim: The guideline Work Group was co-chaired by John A Kellum and Norbert Lameire.
claims.evidence: John A Kellum, MD, FCCM, FACP, Work Group Co-Chair Norbert Lameire, MD, PhD, Work Group Co-Chair

claims.claim: The guideline's reference list (references 1-155 in this section) cites the primary epidemiology, RIFLE/AKIN classification, fluid resuscitation, vasopressor, and glycaemic control literature underpinning the recommendations.
claims.evidence: References Kidney International Supplements (2012) 2, 124–138; doi:10.1038/kisup.2011.38 1. Chertow GM, Burdick E, Honour M, et al. Acute kidney injury, mortality, length of stay, and costs in hospitalized patients.

claims.claim: The ARFTN RCT randomized 1124 ICU patients with AKI to intensive vs less-intensive RRT across 27 North-American centers.
claims.evidence: The Veterans Affairs/National Institutes of Health Acute Renal Failure Trial Network (ARFTN) study563 was a RCT assessing the effects of intensive compared to less-intensive RRT in 1124 ICU patients with AKI in 27 Veterans Affairs– and university-affiliated North-American centers.

claims.claim: In ARFTN, intermittent treatments were prescribed at Kt/V 1.4 with delivered Kt/V averaging 1.3, given 3x/week (less-intensive) or 6x/week (more-intensive), giving weekly Kt/V ~3.9 vs ~6.5.
claims.evidence: Intermittent treatments were prescribed at a Kt/V of 1.4, with a delivered Kt/V averaging 1.3, and were performed three (less-intensive arm) or six (more-intensive arm) times per week. Consequently, the weekly Kt/V was approximately 6.5 in the intensive and 3.9 in the less-intensive arm.

claims.claim: Limitations of ARFTN include predominance of males and nonstandardized timing for initiating RRT.
claims.evidence: Limitations of this study include the predominance of males, and the nonstandardized timing for initiating RRT.

claims.claim: The Hannover Dialysis Outcome Study compared SLED targeting plasma urea 120-150 mg/dl vs <90 mg/dl in 148 ICU patients with AKI.
claims.evidence: randomized 148 ICU patients with AKI to two different doses of SLED: a standard-dialysis arm dosed to maintain plasma urea levels between 120–150 mg/dl (20–25 mmol/l), or an intensified- dialysis arm dosed to maintain plasma urea levels o90 mg/dl (o15 mmol/l)

claims.claim: In CKD, mortality risk decreased 7% per 0.1 higher delivered Kt/V, but no further decrease above Kt/V 1.3.
claims.evidence: a strong association between the delivered IHD dose and mortality, with a decreased mortality risk of 7% for each 0.1 higher level of delivered Kt/V in CKD patients. However, above a Kt/V of 1.3, no further decrease in mortality was noted.

claims.claim: Seven RCTs have investigated the role of CRRT dose in AKI.
claims.evidence: Seven RCTs have investigated the role of CRRT dose in AKI (Suppl Tables 37 and 38).

claims.claim: ARFTN compared standard-intensity predilution CVVHDF at 20 ml/kg/h with high-intensity CVVHDF at 35 ml/kg/h, with >95% of the prescribed dose delivered in the less-intensive group.
claims.evidence: compared standard-intensity predilution CVVHDF with a prescribed effluent flow of 20 ml/kg/h to high-intensity CVVHDF at 35 ml/kg/h. As dis- cussed in Recommendation 5.8.3 rationale, there were no differences in outcomes between the two study arms. Importantly, more than 95% of the prescribed dose of CRRT was delivered in the less-intensive group.

claims.claim: The RENAL study compared postdilution CVVHDF at 25 vs 40 ml/kg/h in 1464 AKI patients in 35 Australian and New Zealand centers with no difference in 28- or 90-day mortality.
claims.evidence: It compared the effects of postdilution CVVHDF at doses of 25 and 40 ml/kg/h on 28- and 90-day mortality rates in 1464 AKI patients. The delivered dose was 88% and 84% of prescribed in the low- and high-dose groups, respectively. As in the ARFTN study, there was no difference in 28- or 90-day mortality between the two groups.

claims.claim: If the target RRT dose is not achieved despite optimizing the initial modality, a switch to or combination of another modality should be considered.
claims.evidence: In patients who do not achieve the target dose of RRT, despite optimization of the initial modality, a switch to another modality or the combination of different modalities should be considered.

claims.claim: There are insufficient data to recommend elevated RRT doses in patients with AKI and septic shock.
claims.evidence: Although there are insufficient data supporting a recommendation for elevated RRT doses in patients with AKI and septic shock, limited data suggest that a higher dose might be beneficial in some patients.

claims.claim: Whether subgroups such as hypercatabolic AKI patients benefit from higher doses requires further investigation.
claims.evidence: Whether specific subgroups of AKI patients, such as those with hypercatabolism, may benefit from higher doses will require further investigation.

claims.claim: Studies in CRRT show delivery usually falls substantially short of the prescribed dose.
claims.evidence: As in chronic dialysis, studies in CRRT have shown that delivery usually falls substantially short of the prescribed dose.782

claims.claim: This part of source_006 is the guideline reference/bibliography list (refs 156–360), not narrative recommendation text.
claims.evidence: Kidney International Supplements (2012) 2, 124–138 r e f e r e n c e s

claims.claim: A meta-analysis found low-dose dopamine increases urine output but does not prevent renal dysfunction or death.
claims.evidence: Friedrich JO, Adhikari N, Herridge MS, et al. Meta-analysis: low-dose dopamine increases urine output but does not prevent renal dysfunction or death. Ann Intern Med 2005; 142: 510–524.

claims.claim: A meta-analysis reported fenoldopam reduces the need for renal replacement therapy and in-hospital death in cardiovascular surgery.
claims.evidence: Landoni G, Biondi-Zoccai GG, Marino G, et al. Fenoldopam reduces the need for renal replacement therapy and in-hospital death in cardiovascular surgery: a meta-analysis. J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2008; 22: 27–33.

claims.claim: Initial low-dose gentamicin for S. aureus bacteremia and endocarditis is nephrotoxic.
claims.evidence: Cosgrove SE, Vigliani GA, Fowler VG, Jr., et al. Initial low-dose gentamicin for Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia and endocarditis is nephrotoxic. Clin Infect Dis 2009; 48: 713–721.

claims.claim: Furosemide did not improve renal recovery after hemofiltration for acute renal failure in critically ill patients in a double blind RCT.
claims.evidence: van der Voort PH, Boerma EC, Koopmans M, et al. Furosemide does not improve renal recovery after hemofiltration for acute renal failure in critically ill patients: a double blind randomized controlled trial.

claims.claim: Early intervention with erythropoietin did not affect the outcome of AKI in the EARLYARF trial.
claims.evidence: Endre ZH, Walker RJ, Pickering JW, et al. Early intervention with erythropoietin does not affect the outcome of acute kidney injury (the EARLYARF trial). Kidney Int 2010; 77: 1020–1030.

claims.claim: Nesiritide carries a risk of worsening renal function in patients with acutely decompensated heart failure.
claims.evidence: Sackner-Bernstein JD, Skopicki HA, Aaronson KD. Risk of worsening renal function with nesiritide in patients with acutely decompensated heart failure. Circulation 2005; 111: 1487–1491.

claims.claim: Prophylactic nesiritide does not prevent dialysis or all-cause mortality in high-risk cardiac surgery.
claims.evidence: Ejaz AA, Martin TD, Johnson RJ, et al. Prophylactic nesiritide does not prevent dialysis or all-cause mortality in patients undergoing high-risk cardiac surgery.

claims.claim: Acute renal failure has been associated with inhaled tobramycin use.
claims.evidence: Cannella CA, Wilkinson ST. Acute renal failure associated with inhaled tobramycin. Am J Health Syst Pharm 2006; 63: 1858–1861.

claims.claim: Caspofungin is less nephrotoxic than amphotericin B in vitro and predominantly damages distal renal tubular cells.
claims.evidence: Wegner B, Baer P, Gauer S, et al. Caspofungin is less nephrotoxic than amphotericin B in vitro and predominantly damages distal renal tubular cells.

claims.claim: A meta-analysis of 10 RCTs in 1100 patients found no advantage for biocompatible or high-flux membranes in AKI.
claims.evidence: A recent meta-analysis of 10 randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials in 1100 patients could not establish any advantage for biocompatible or high-flux membranes.702

claims.claim: KDIGO considers use of either a biocompatible or modified cellulose acetate membrane appropriate.
claims.evidence: we agree with the authors’ conclusion that the use of either a biocompatible or modified cellulose acetate membrane appears to be appropriate.

claims.claim: Coating the AN-69 membrane with polyethyleneimine significantly reduces bradykinin generation.
claims.evidence: Neutralizing the electronegativity of the AN-69 membrane by coating with polyethyleneimine sig- nificantly reduces bradykinin generation.709

claims.claim: Use of RRT to treat sepsis (via mediator removal) should be considered experimental.
claims.evidence: Until further evi- dence becomes available, the use of RRT to treat sepsis should be considered experimental.

claims.claim: KDIGO 5.6.1 (Not Graded): use continuous and intermittent RRT as complementary therapies in AKI patients.
claims.evidence: 5.6.1: Use continuous and intermittent RRT as comple- mentary therapies in AKI patients. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: The Cochrane meta-analysis of 15 RCTs in 1550 AKI patients found similar hospital mortality, ICU mortality, hospital length of stay and renal recovery for CRRT vs IHD.
claims.evidence: This analysis concluded that outcomes were similar in critically ill AKI patients treated with CRRT and IHD for hospital mortality (RR 1.01; 95% CI 0.92–1.12; n ¼ 1245), ICU mortality (RR 1.06; 95% CI 0.90–1.26; n ¼ 515)

claims.claim: Mean arterial pressure at end of treatment was significantly higher with CRRT than IHD (mean deviation 5.35; 95% CI 1.41–9.29).
claims.evidence: the mean arterial pressure at the end of the treatment was significantly higher with CRRT than with IHD (mean deviation 5.35; 95% CI 1.41–9.29; n ¼ 112)

claims.claim: KDIGO 5.6.2 (2B): suggest CRRT rather than standard intermittent RRT for hemodynamically unstable patients.
claims.evidence: 5.6.2: We suggest using CRRT, rather than standard intermittent RRT, for hemodynamically unstable patients. (2B)

claims.claim: KDIGO 5.6.3 (2B): suggest CRRT rather than intermittent RRT for AKI patients with acute brain injury or increased intracranial pressure or generalized brain edema.
claims.evidence: 5.6.3: We suggest using CRRT, rather than intermittent RRT, for AKI patients with acute brain injury or other causes of increased intracranial pressure or generalized brain edema. (2B)

claims.claim: Contraindications to PD in AKI include extremely high catabolism, severe respiratory failure, severe ileus, intra-abdominal hypertension, recent abdominal surgery, and diaphragmatic peritoneum-pleura connections.
claims.evidence: Extremely high catabolism, severe respiratory failure, severe ileus, intra-abdominal hypertension, recent abdominal surgery and diaphragmatic peritoneum-pleura connections are contraindications to PD.

claims.claim: Severe AKI occurs in less than 1% of hospitalized children and 4.5% of children admitted to intensive care.
claims.evidence: severe AKI is relatively rare in children compared to adults, occurring in less than 1% of hospitalized children740 and only 4.5% of children admitted to an intensive care unit,741

claims.claim: The extracorporeal circuit volume can exceed 15% of a small pediatric patient's total blood volume, making accurate ultrafiltration and blood flow rates crucial.
claims.evidence: since the extracorporeal circuit volume can comprise more than 15% of a small pediatric patient’s total blood volume, and small ultrafiltration inaccuracies may represent a large percentage of a small pediatric patient’s total body water.

claims.claim: Convective modalities were associated with increased survival in children with stem-cell transplants receiving CRRT (59% vs 27%, P<0.05).
claims.evidence: convective modalities were associated with increased survival in children with stem-cell transplants in a prospective cohort study (59% vs. 27%, Po0.05).747

claims.claim: Barenbrock RCT in 117 AKI patients: bicarbonate replacement fluid gave better correction of acidosis, lower lactate, and fewer cardiovascular events than lactate.
claims.evidence: Barenbrock et al.751 rando- mized 117 AKI patients to CVVH with lactate or bicarbonate replacement fluid. The use of bicarbonate resulted in better correction of acidosis and lower lactate levels.

claims.claim: KDIGO 5.7.4 (1B): dialysis and replacement fluids in AKI must at minimum comply with AAMI standards for bacteria and endotoxins.
claims.evidence: 5.7.4: We recommend that dialysis fluids and replacement fluids in patients with AKI, at a minimum, comply with American Association of Medical Instrumen- tation (AAMI) standards regarding contamination with bacteria and endotoxins. (1B)

claims.claim: KDIGO 5.8.3 (1A): deliver a Kt/V of 3.9 per week when using intermittent or extended RRT in AKI.
claims.evidence: 5.8.3: We recommend delivering a Kt/V of 3.9 per week when using intermittent or extended RRT in AKI. (1A)

claims.claim: KDIGO 5.8.4 (1A): deliver an effluent volume of 20–25 ml/kg/h for CRRT in AKI, usually requiring a higher prescription.
claims.evidence: 5.8.4: We recommend delivering an effluent volume of 20–25 ml/kg/h for CRRT in AKI (1A). This will usually require a higher prescription of effluent volume. (Not Graded)

claims.claim: Kt/V urea has important limitations in AKI because patients are metabolically unstable and urea volume of distribution exceeds total body water.
claims.evidence: AKI patients are metabolically unstable, with variations in urea generation. In addition, their urea volume of distribution appears to exceed the patient’s total body-water volume.775

claims.claim: Delivered RRT dose in AKI is frequently smaller than prescribed and even below the recommended minimum for CKD.
claims.evidence: Several clinical investigations have shown that the actual delivered dose of RRT in AKI patients is frequently smaller than the prescribed dose, and even smaller than the recommended minimum for CKD patients.771,773,776–778

claims.claim: Impediments to adequate RRT dose delivery include hemodynamic instability, patient size, access problems, technical problems, transport needs, and early filter clotting.
claims.evidence: Impediments to adequate dose delivery were hemodynamic instability, patient size, access problems, technical problems, need for patient transportation, and early filter clotting.

claims.claim: In the Schiffl trial, daily IHD delivered weekly Kt/V 5.8±0.6 vs 3±0.6 for alternate-day IHD and lowered mortality 28% vs 46%.
claims.evidence: The daily arm received a weekly Kt/V approximately two times higher than the alternate-day arm (5.8 ± 0.6 vs. 3 ± 0.6, respectively). Daily IHD resulted in lower mortality (28% vs. 46%, P ¼ 0.01)

claims.claim: Typical CVVH settings for a 70-kg patient are blood flow 150–250 ml/min with ultrafiltrate 1500–2000 ml/h and effluent 36–48 l/d.
claims.evidence: CVVH ... Blood flow (ml/min) ... 150–250 ... Ultrafiltrate (ml/h) 100–300 1500–2000 ... Effluent volume (l/d) 2–8 36–48

claims.claim: N-acetylcysteine has been reported not to artifactually lower plasma creatinine concentration.
claims.evidence: 368. Haase M, Haase-Fielitz A, Ratnaike S, et al. N-Acetylcysteine does not artifactually lower plasma creatinine concentration. Nephrol Dial Transplant 2008; 23: 1581–1587.

claims.claim: Anaphylactoid reactions, including fatal ones, have been reported with intravenous N-acetylcysteine.
claims.evidence: 375. Appelboam AV, Dargan PI, Knighton J. Fatal anaphylactoid reaction to N-acetylcysteine: caution in patients with asthma. Emerg Med J 2002; 19: 594–595.

claims.claim: Serum creatinine fluctuates in the absence of iodinated contrast material, complicating studies of contrast nephrotoxicity.
claims.evidence: 388. Newhouse JH, Kho D, Rao QA, et al. Frequency of serum creatinine changes in the absence of iodinated contrast material: implications for studies of contrast nephrotoxicity. AJR Am J Roentgenol 2008; 191: 376–382.

claims.claim: The rate of contrast-induced nephropathy reported depends on the definition used.
claims.evidence: 391. Jabara R, Gadesam RR, Pendyala LK, et al. Impact of the definition utilized on the rate of contrast-induced nephropathy in percutaneous coronary intervention. Am J Cardiol 2009; 103: 1657–1662.

claims.claim: A simple risk score has been developed to predict contrast-induced nephropathy after percutaneous coronary intervention.
claims.evidence: 418. Mehran R, Aymong ED, Nikolsky E, et al. A simple risk score for prediction of contrast-induced nephropathy after percutaneous coronary intervention: development and initial validation. J Am Coll Cardiol 2004; 44: 1393–1399.

claims.claim: Meta-analysis compared the relative nephrotoxicity of high- versus low-osmolality iodinated contrast media.
claims.evidence: 449. Barrett BJ, Carlisle EJ. Metaanalysis of the relative nephrotoxicity of high- and low-osmolality iodinated contrast media. Radiology 1993; 188: 171–178.

claims.claim: Nephrotoxicity of iso-osmolar versus low-osmolar contrast media was reported as equal in low-risk patients.
claims.evidence: 451. Feldkamp T, Baumgart D, Elsner M, et al. Nephrotoxicity of iso-osmolar versus low-osmolar contrast media is equal in low risk patients. Clin Nephrol 2006; 66: 322–330.

claims.claim: Prophylactic hemodialysis after radiocontrast media in patients with renal insufficiency is potentially harmful.
claims.evidence: 518. Vogt B, Ferrari P, Schonholzer C, et al. Prophylactic hemodialysis after radiocontrast media in patients with renal insufficiency is potentially harmful. Am J Med 2001; 111: 692–698.

claims.claim: One retrospective cohort reported sodium bicarbonate was associated with an increased incidence of contrast nephropathy.
claims.evidence: 489. From AM, Bartholmai BJ, Williams AW, et al. Sodium bicarbonate is associated with an increased incidence of contrast nephropathy: a retrospective cohort study of 7977 patients at mayo clinic.

claims.claim: Oral hydration with alkalinization was reported noninferior to intravenous therapy for prevention of contrast-induced nephropathy in CKD.
claims.evidence: 493. Cho R, Javed N, Traub D, et al. Oral hydration and alkalinization is noninferior to intravenous therapy for prevention of contrast-induced nephropathy in patients with chronic kidney disease.

claims.claim: Fluid overload before continuous hemofiltration was associated with survival in critically ill children.
claims.evidence: 543. Foland JA, Fortenberry JD, Warshaw BL, et al. Fluid overload before continuous hemofiltration and survival in critically ill children: a retrospective analysis. Crit Care Med 2004; 32: 1771–1776.

claims.claim: Plasma NGAL was reported as an early biomarker for acute kidney injury in an adult ICU population.
claims.evidence: 551. Cruz DN, de Cal M, Garzotto F, et al. Plasma neutrophil gelatinase- associated lipocalin is an early biomarker for acute kidney injury in an adult ICU population. Intensive Care Med 2010; 36: 444–451.

claims.claim: Regional citrate anticoagulation was reported superior to systemic heparin in critically ill patients on CVVHDF.
claims.evidence: 601b. Park JS, Kim GH, Kang CM, et al. Regional anticoagulation with citrate is superior to systemic anticoagulation with heparin in critically ill patients undergoing continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration. Korean J Intern Med 2011; 26: 68–75.

claims.claim: Citrate versus heparin during venovenous hemofiltration gave similar hemofilter survival but significantly less bleeding in patients at low bleeding risk.
claims.evidence: 601. Betjes MG, van Oosterom D, van Agteren M, et al. Regional citrate versus heparin anticoagulation during venovenous hemofiltration in patients at low risk for bleeding: similar hemofilter survival but significantly less bleeding.

claims.claim: Citrate metabolism is impaired in acute hepatic failure.
claims.evidence: 608. Apsner R, Schwarzenhofer M, Derfler K, et al. Impairment of citrate metabolism in acute hepatic failure. Wien Klin Wochenschr 1997; 109: 123–127.

claims.claim: Increased total to ionized calcium ratio occurs during CVVHD with regional citrate anticoagulation and can detect citrate overdose.
claims.evidence: 612. Meier-Kriesche HU, Gitomer J, Finkel K, et al. Increased total to ionized calcium ratio during continuous venovenous hemodialysis with regional citrate anticoagulation.

claims.claim: Nafamostat mesilate is used as a regional anticoagulant for hemodialysis in patients at high risk for bleeding.
claims.evidence: 591. Akizawa T, Koshikawa S, Ota K, et al. Nafamostat mesilate: a regional anticoagulant for hemodialysis in patients at high risk for bleeding. Nephron 1993; 64: 376–381.

claims.claim: Nafamostat mesilate can cause hyperkalemia, agranulocytosis and anaphylactoid reactions.
claims.evidence: 595. Muto S, Imai M, Asano Y. Mechanisms of hyperkalemia caused by nafamostat mesilate. Gen Pharmacol 1995; 26: 1627–1632. 596. Okada H, Suzuki H, Deguchi N, et al. Agranulocytosis in a haemodialysed patient induced by a proteinase inhibitor, nafamostate mesilate.

claims.claim: Internal jugular access is superior to subclavian access for temporary dialysis catheters.
claims.evidence: 650. Cimochowski GE, Worley E, Rutherford WE, et al. Superiority of the internal jugular over the subclavian access for temporary dialysis. Nephron 1990; 54: 154–161.

claims.claim: A randomized controlled trial compared femoral versus jugular venous catheterization and risk of nosocomial events in adults requiring acute renal replacement therapy.
claims.evidence: 658. Parienti JJ, Thirion M, Megarbane B, et al. Femoral vs jugular venous catheterization and risk of nosocomial events in adults requiring acute renal replacement therapy: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA 2008; 299: 2413–2422.

claims.claim: Real-time ultrasound guidance for internal jugular catheterization increases success rates and reduces complications compared with the landmark technique.
claims.evidence: 671. Leung J, Duffy M, Finckh A. Real-time ultrasonographically-guided internal jugular vein catheterization in the emergency department increases success rates and reduces complications: a randomized, prospective study.

claims.claim: Antimicrobial lock solutions reduce hemodialysis catheter-related bacteraemia.
claims.evidence: 684. Labriola L, Crott R, Jadoul M. Preventing haemodialysis catheter-related bacteraemia with an antimicrobial lock solution: a meta-analysis of prospective randomized trials. Nephrol Dial Transplant 2008; 23: 1666–1672.

claims.claim: AN-69 membrane reactions are pH-dependent and preventable.
claims.evidence: 703. Brophy PD, Mottes TA, Kudelka TL, et al. AN-69 membrane reactions are pH-dependent and preventable. Am J Kidney Dis 2001; 38: 173–178.

claims.claim: Anaphylactoid reactions occur during hemodialysis on AN69 membranes in patients receiving ACE inhibitors.
claims.evidence: 708. Tielemans C, Madhoun P, Lenaers M, et al. Anaphylactoid reactions during hemodialysis on AN69 membranes in patients receiving ACE inhibitors. Kidney Int 1990; 38: 982–984.

claims.claim: Continuous renal replacement therapy was associated with less chronic renal failure than intermittent haemodialysis after acute renal failure.
claims.evidence: 720. Bell M, Granath F, Schon S, et al. Continuous renal replacement therapy is associated with less chronic renal failure than intermittent haemodialysis after acute renal failure. Intensive Care Med 2007; 33: 773–780.

claims.claim: Intermittent dialysis had lower costs than continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration for acute renal failure in the ICU.
claims.evidence: 717. Farese S, Jakob SM, Kalicki R, et al. Treatment of acute renal failure in the intensive care unit: lower costs by intermittent dialysis than continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration. Artif Organs 2009; 33: 634–640.

claims.claim: Blood-primed CRRT circuits with zero balance ultrafiltration achieve electrolyte and acid-base homeostasis prior to patient connection.
claims.evidence: 704. Hackbarth RM, Eding D, Gianoli Smith C, et al. Zero balance ultrafiltration (Z-BUF) in blood-primed CRRT circuits achieves electrolyte and acid-base homeostasis prior to patient connection.

claims.claim: Tenckhoff catheters were superior to Cook catheters in pediatric acute peritoneal dialysis.
claims.evidence: 689. Chadha V, Warady BA, Blowey DL, et al. Tenckhoff catheters prove superior to cook catheters in pediatric acute peritoneal dialysis. Am J Kidney Dis 2000; 35: 1111–1116.

claims.claim: Severe acute renal failure impacts the frequency of withdrawal from acute care.
claims.evidence: 565. Swartz R, Perry E, Daley J. The frequency of withdrawal from acute care is impacted by severe acute renal failure. J Palliat Med 2004; 7: 676–682.

claims.claim: Continuous venovenous hemofiltration can be performed without anticoagulation in high-risk patients.
claims.evidence: 574. Tan HK, Baldwin I, Bellomo R. Continuous veno-venous hemofiltration without anticoagulation in high-risk patients. Intensive Care Med 2000; 26: 1652–1657.

# Acute Kidney Injury (project `aki-v2`) — Human Review Artifact

**Status:** `research validation` = **FAIL (draft)**, sign-off: no. This document is the review packet for a human curator: it lists every executable criterion, every decision that blocks sign-off, and the coverage gaps. Numbers below were re-derived from the current graph; nothing is carried forward from earlier drafts.

---

## 1. Executive summary

The `aki-v2` graph is a condition-mode knowledge graph for **acute kidney injury**, built from seven sources. Current size, quoted from **`research validation` as the single source of truth** for all metrics in this report: **551 nodes, 756 edges, 480 claims, 120 `defines` edges, OMOP mapping rate 0.405 (0 confirmed), 46 concept-fallback nodes, 11 conflicts of which 5 remain open.** `research validation mode=summary` reports the mapping coverage differently ("192/551 nodes OMOP-mapped", i.e. 0.349), and `research validation`'s own warning line names 269 unmapped nodes (implying 282/551 = 0.512); the three figures do not reconcile and the discrepancy is raised as a decision item, **D-15 (§4.6)**. Only the `research validation` `mapping_rate` figure is quoted elsewhere in this document.

The definitional backbone is tier-1: KDIGO 2012 supplies the normative AKI definition and staging table ("AKI is defined as any of the following (Not Graded): Increase in SCr by ≥0.3 mg/dl (≥26.5 µmol/l) within 48 hours") [source_006] rec 2.1.1, and NICE NG148 supplies the UK detection thresholds ("a rise in serum creatinine of 26 micromol/litre or greater within 48 hours") [source_007] rec 1.3.1. Five tier-3 papers contribute study-local operationalisations: an AKIN-based persistent-AKI biomarker study [source_001], a murine trametinib efficacy study [source_002], a perioperative AKI prediction study [source_003], a persistent-AKI-stage-3 ICU prediction study [source_004], and a heart-failure-after-AKI cohort study [source_005].

Most connected concepts in the graph are Acute Kidney Injury (degree 211), Contrast-induced acute kidney injury (76), Serum creatinine (58), Renal replacement therapy (34), AKI Stage 3 (27), Trametinib (24), Mortality (21), Postoperative acute kidney injury (21), Urine output (19) and Continuous renal replacement therapy (19).

## 3. Exclusions, risk factors and graded recommendations

Exclusions in the graph are of two kinds: study-local cohort exclusions from the tier-3 papers [source_003] [source_004] [source_005], and definitional exclusions asserted by the tier-1 guideline [source_006]. Risk factors come predominantly from the two tier-1 guidelines [source_006] [source_007], with supporting observations from the tier-3 papers [source_001] [source_003] [source_005].

The [source_003] exclusion set is "pediatric patients under the age of 18, individuals who underwent cardiac surgery, and those who were diagnosed with end-stage renal disease or had preoperative creatinine levels exceeding 4.5 mg/dL" [source_003]. [source_005] excludes "baseline eGFR < 15 ml/min/1.37m2, kidney transplantation, end-stage renal disease (ESRD), or receipt of dialysis prior to the AKI ascertainment window, and age < 18 years at HF diagnosis" [source_005].
